statutes.t: Scope of Article
statutes.part: Article 1, Part 1 - General Provisions
x: Article 1 applies to a transaction only to the extent that the transaction is governed by another article of the UCC (for this course, Article 2).
c: Article 1's general rules (definitions, good faith, course of dealing, and so on) apply only when some other UCC article governs the deal. If the deal is outside the UCC (a services contract, a real estate sale), Article 1 does not apply on its own force.

statutes.t: Construction to Promote Purposes and Policies; Supplemental Principles of Law
statutes.part: Article 1, Part 1 - General Provisions
x: The UCC must be liberally construed and applied to promote its underlying purposes and policies, which are: (1) to simplify, clarify, and modernize the law governing commercial transactions; (2) to permit the continued expansion of commercial practices through custom, usage, and agreement of the parties; and (3) to make uniform the law among the various jurisdictions.

Unless displaced by particular UCC provisions, the principles of law and equity supplement the Code - including the law merchant and the law of capacity to contract, principal and agent, estoppel, fraud, misrepresentation, duress, coercion, mistake, bankruptcy, and other validating or invalidating causes.
c: The Code is meant to be semi-permanent and flexible, so courts apply it to new circumstances and practices. Each section is read in light of its purpose and the Code as a whole, and its language is construed narrowly or broadly as those purposes require.

Supplemental principles of common law and equity may supplement the Code but may not supplant it. The Code preempts common law and equity that is inconsistent with either its text or its purposes and policies - displacement is not limited to cases where a provision "explicitly" displaces other law (the old Comment's "explicitly displaced" wording was wrong). Supplemental law can evolve with technology (electronic contracting, automated "electronic agents").

When the other law is a statute, subsection (b) still guides the analysis, but ordinary rules on how statutes interact also apply. An equitable principle does not gain extra force just because it is codified; but a statute meant to give extra protection to a class of people (for example, consumers) may control even if it conflicts with the UCC.
The list in (b) is illustrative, not exclusive. "Bankruptcy" means general principles of insolvency law, federal or state.

statutes.t: General Definitions (selected)
statutes.part: Article 1, Part 2 - General Definitions and Principles of Interpretation
x: Unless the context otherwise requires, terms defined here or in other articles have the stated meanings; (b) is subject to definitions in other articles that apply to particular articles or parts.
(b)(3) Agreement

"Agreement," as distinguished from "contract," means the bargain of the parties in fact, as found in their language or inferred from other circumstances, including course of performance, course of dealing, or usage of trade as provided in § 1-303.
(b)(8) Burden of establishing
The "burden of establishing" a fact means the burden of persuading the trier of fact that the existence of the fact is more probable than its nonexistence.
(b)(9) Buyer in ordinary course of business

A person that buys goods in good faith, without knowledge that the sale violates the rights of another person in the goods, and in the ordinary course from a person (other than a pawnbroker) in the business of selling goods of that kind. The sale must comport with the usual or customary practices of that kind of business or the seller's own usual practices. Payment may be cash, exchange, or secured or unsecured credit. Only a buyer that takes possession of the goods or has a right to recover them from the seller under Article 2 can qualify; a person that acquires goods in a bulk transfer or as security for or in total or partial satisfaction of a money debt is not a buyer in ordinary course.
(b)(10) Conspicuous

A term is "conspicuous" if it is so written, displayed, or presented that, based on the totality of the circumstances, a reasonable person against which it is to operate ought to have noticed it. Whether a term is conspicuous is a decision for the court. Conspicuous terms include (A) a heading in capitals equal to or greater in size than the surrounding text, or in contrasting type, font, or color; and (B) body language in larger type than the surrounding text, or in contrasting type, font, or color, or set off by symbols or other marks that call attention to it.
(b)(12) Contract
"Contract," as distinguished from "agreement," means the total legal obligation that results from the parties' agreement as determined by the UCC as supplemented by any other applicable laws.
(b)(20) Good faith
Except as otherwise provided in Article 5, "good faith" means honesty in fact and the observance of reasonable commercial standards of fair dealing.
(b)(23) Insolvent

(A) having generally ceased to pay debts in the ordinary course of business other than as a result of a bona fide dispute; (B) being unable to pay debts as they become due; or (C) being insolvent within the meaning of federal bankruptcy law.
(b)(29) Purchase
Taking by sale, lease, discount, negotiation, mortgage, pledge, lien, security interest, issue or reissue, gift, or any other voluntary transaction creating an interest in property.
(b)(30) Purchaser
A person that takes by purchase.
(b)(31) Record
Information that is inscribed on a tangible medium or that is stored in an electronic or other medium and is retrievable in perceivable form.
(b)(35) Security interest

An interest in personal property or fixtures which secures payment or performance of an obligation. It does not include a buyer's special property on identification of goods under § 2-401. Whether a transaction in the form of a lease creates a security interest is determined under § 1-203.
(b)(37) Sign / Signed

"Signed" includes using any symbol executed or adopted with present intention to adopt or accept a writing. "Sign" means, with present intent to authenticate or adopt a record: (A) execute or adopt a tangible symbol; or (B) attach to or logically associate with the record an electronic symbol, sound, or process.
(b)(40) Term
A portion of an agreement that relates to a particular matter.
(b)(43) Writing
Includes printing, typewriting, or any other intentional reduction to tangible form. "Written" has a corresponding meaning.
c: "Agreement" fully includes usage of trade, course of dealing, course of performance, and the surrounding circumstances, plus any agreement the Code allows to displace a stated rule of law. Whether an agreement has legal consequences is decided by the Code and, through § 1-103, by contract law.
"Buyer in ordinary course of business" matters most in § 2-403 (entrustment) and Article 9.

"Conspicuous" asks whether a reasonable person against which the term operates ought to have noticed it; the court decides, case by case, on the totality of the circumstances. The 2022 amendments dropped the old type-size examples from the text and moved a broader list of factors to the comment: (i) headings and text that contrast with the surrounding text (bold capitals do not help if everything around them is also bold capitals); (ii) placement - at the start of the record or near where the person assents is better than buried in the middle; (iii) hyperlinks - language drawing attention to the link and its function; (iv) the heading's wording - a misleading heading such as "Warranty" over a disclaimer can defeat conspicuousness; (v) the effort needed to reach the term (multiple links is worse); (vi) separate assent or acknowledgment of the term is generally enough. The reasonable person varies with the market (large business, small business, consumer).
"Contract" is unchanged in substance from former § 1-201.

"Good faith" once meant only honesty in fact, with a merchant-only objective standard in former § 2-103(1)(b). The definition now applies to everyone (except in Article 5): subjective honesty in fact plus objective observance of reasonable commercial standards of fair dealing. "Fair dealing" concerns the fairness of conduct, not the care with which an act is performed - a different concept from ordinary care.
The three insolvency tests are alternatives and are applied from a commercial standpoint.
"Purchase" now uses "means" instead of "includes."
"Record" is taken from Article 9's definition.

A complete signature is not necessary. A symbol may be printed, stamped, written, or electronically attached; it may be initials, a thumbprint, or an electronic symbol, sound, or process; it may appear anywhere, including a billhead or letterhead. The question is always whether it was executed or adopted with present intention to authenticate or adopt the record. A "writing" is signed only by a tangible symbol; an electronically signed record that is later printed is not a signed writing until someone acts with present intent to adopt the printout.
"Term" is unchanged from former § 1-201.

statutes.t: Notice; Knowledge
statutes.part: Article 1, Part 2 - General Definitions and Principles of Interpretation
x: Subject to (f), a person has "notice" of a fact if the person (1) has actual knowledge of it; (2) has received a notice or notification of it; or (3) from all the facts and circumstances known at the time, has reason to know that it exists.
"Knowledge" means actual knowledge; "knows" has a corresponding meaning.
"Discover," "learn," and similar words refer to knowledge rather than reason to know.
A person "notifies" or "gives" a notice by taking steps reasonably required to inform the other person in ordinary course, whether or not the other person actually comes to know of it.

Subject to (f), a person "receives" a notice when (1) it comes to that person's attention; or (2) it is duly delivered in a form reasonable under the circumstances at the place of business through which the contract was made or another location held out as the place for receipt.

Notice received by an organization is effective for a transaction from the time it is brought to the attention of the individual conducting that transaction, and in any event from the time it would have been if the organization had exercised due diligence (reasonable routines for passing on significant information, reasonably complied with).
c: A person has notice of a fact when, among other ways, the person has received a notification of it.
"Notifies" is used when the key fact is proper dispatch of the notice, not receipt. When receipt matters, the Code says so; (e) states when a notice is received.
Notice received by a clerk in Department A is effective for a transaction run by Department B only from when it was or should have been passed to the person running that transaction.

statutes.t: Reasonable Time; Seasonableness
statutes.part: Article 1, Part 2 - General Definitions and Principles of Interpretation
x: Whether a time for taking an action required by the UCC is reasonable depends on the nature, purpose, and circumstances of the action.
An action is taken "seasonably" if it is taken at or within the time agreed or, if no time is agreed, at or within a reasonable time.
c: "Reasonable time" is judged in the transactional context of the particular action.

The agreement fixing the time need not be part of the main agreement. Because "agreement" includes course of dealing, usage of trade, and course of performance, those circumstances often matter in deciding what is a reasonable time.
statutes.note: Not to be confused with former § 1-205 (course of dealing and usage of trade), which is now § 1-303. Class slides cite the old number.

statutes.t: Variation by Agreement
statutes.part: Article 1, Part 3 - Territorial Applicability and General Rules
x: Except as otherwise provided in (b) or elsewhere in the UCC, the effect of UCC provisions may be varied by agreement.

The obligations of good faith, diligence, reasonableness, and care prescribed by the UCC may not be disclaimed by agreement. The parties may by agreement set the standards by which performance of those obligations is measured if the standards are not manifestly unreasonable. Whenever the UCC requires action within a reasonable time, the parties may fix any time that is not manifestly unreasonable.
The phrase "unless otherwise agreed" in some provisions does not imply that other provisions cannot be varied by agreement under this section.
c: Freedom of contract is a basic UCC principle: parties can change the legal consequences of Code provisions, but not the meaning of the statute itself or of its defined terms (for example, "holder in due course"). Agreements cannot destroy third parties' rights. Some exceptions are explicit and some come from a fair reading - for example, the statute of frauds (§ 2-201) cannot be waived orally as part of the very contract it makes unenforceable. Good faith, diligence, reasonableness, and care cannot be disclaimed, but parties may set standards for measuring them unless manifestly unreasonable. A fair agreed time is the strongest evidence of a reasonable time; only a time so unreasonable that it effectively eliminates all remedy is disregarded, judged as of contracting.
Parties may vary the Code by writing their own rules or by adopting a recognized body of rules (for example, UNIDROIT Principles or a trade code).
"Unless otherwise agreed" was used only to avoid argument; its absence carries no negative implication, because the residual rule is that all Code provisions may be varied by agreement.

statutes.t: Course of Performance, Course of Dealing, and Usage of Trade
statutes.part: Article 1, Part 3 - Territorial Applicability and General Rules
x: A "course of performance" is a sequence of conduct between the parties to a particular transaction that exists if (1) the agreement involves repeated occasions for performance by a party; and (2) the other party, with knowledge of the nature of the performance and opportunity for objection, accepts the performance or acquiesces in it without objection.

A "course of dealing" is a sequence of conduct concerning previous transactions between the parties that is fairly to be regarded as establishing a common basis of understanding for interpreting their expressions and other conduct.

A "usage of trade" is any practice or method of dealing having such regularity of observance in a place, vocation, or trade as to justify an expectation that it will be observed in the transaction in question. Its existence and scope must be proved as facts. If it is embodied in a trade code or similar record, interpreting the record is a question of law.

A course of performance, course of dealing, or usage of trade in the trade in which the parties are engaged or of which they are or should be aware is relevant in ascertaining the meaning of the agreement, may give particular meaning to specific terms, and may supplement or qualify the terms. A usage of trade where part of the performance is to occur may be used as to that part.

Except as provided in (f), express terms and any course of performance, course of dealing, or usage of trade must be construed whenever reasonable as consistent with each other. If that is unreasonable: (1) express terms prevail over course of performance, course of dealing, and usage of trade; (2) course of performance prevails over course of dealing and usage of trade; and (3) course of dealing prevails over usage of trade.
Subject to § 2-209, a course of performance is relevant to show a waiver or modification of any term inconsistent with the course of performance.
Evidence of a usage of trade offered by one party is not admissible unless that party gave the other party notice the court finds sufficient to prevent unfair surprise.
c: The UCC rejects both the "lay-dictionary" and the "conveyancer's" reading of a commercial agreement. Meaning comes from the parties' language and conduct, read in light of commercial practices and surrounding circumstances, which may explain and supplement even a formal or final writing.

Course of dealing is limited to conduct before the agreement; conduct after or under the agreement is course of performance. Course of dealing may enter the agreement by express terms or tacit recognition.

Usage of trade is a guide to the commercial meaning of the agreement; the Code rejects cases treating custom as an attempt to displace established rules of law. Mandatory rules such as the statute of frauds cannot be changed by usage, but gap-filling rules (Part 3 of Article 2) yield to it, because they apply only "unless otherwise agreed."

A usage needs only "regularity of observance" - not that it be ancient, immemorial, or universal. New usages and those followed by the great majority of decent dealers count, even if corner-cutting dissidents disagree. Trade-code usages also count.

The unconscionability policies (§§ 1-304, 2-302) apply to implied terms resting on usage. Commercial acceptance makes out a prima facie case that a usage is reasonable, but courts still police an unconscionable or dishonest practice that has become standard.
Usages bind parties who "are or should be aware" of them; they may be general or particular to a special branch of trade.
Express mention of these elements in some sections does not imply they are excluded elsewhere; "agreement" always includes them.

If a usage clearly varies a general rule but the exact amount is not settled, the party relying on it gets at least the minimum variation shown; if a dominant pattern is shown, that party may go to the trier of fact on whether it was incorporated.
The notice requirement in (g) keeps usage evidence from being used to unfairly surprise the other side.
statutes.note: Replaces former § 1-205 (course of dealing, usage of trade) and former § 2-208 (course of performance). Class slides still cite the old numbers.

statutes.t: Obligation of Good Faith
statutes.part: Article 1, Part 3 - Territorial Applicability and General Rules
x: Every contract or duty within the UCC imposes an obligation of good faith in its performance and enforcement.
c: Good faith runs through the whole Code and applies to the performance or enforcement of every contract or duty, not only where a section mentions it. It does not support an independent cause of action. Instead, failing to perform or enforce a specific contract duty in good faith is a breach of that contract, or makes a remedial right or power unavailable. The doctrine directs courts to interpret contracts in their commercial context; it does not create a separate, free-standing duty of fairness and reasonableness that can be breached on its own.
"Performance and enforcement" include exercising rights created by the Code.

statutes.t: Option to Accelerate at Will
statutes.part: Article 1, Part 3 - Territorial Applicability and General Rules
x: A term letting a party accelerate payment or performance, or require collateral, "at will" or when it "deems itself insecure" (or similar words) means the party may do so only if it in good faith believes that the prospect of payment or performance is impaired. The burden of establishing lack of good faith is on the party against which the power was exercised.
c: The section keeps acceleration clauses from being read as giving one party a power to act on whim or caprice, which could make the deal void, illusory, or too indefinite. The option may be exercised only on a good faith belief that payment or performance is impaired. It does not apply to demand instruments or obligations that by nature may be called at any time; it applies only to obligations first due at a future date.

statutes.t: Scope; Hybrid Transactions; Security and Other Transactions Excluded
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 1 - Short Title, General Construction and Subject Matter
x: Unless the context otherwise requires, and except as provided in (3), Article 2 applies to transactions in goods and, in a hybrid transaction, to the extent provided in (2).

In a hybrid transaction: (a) if the sale-of-goods aspects do not predominate, only the provisions of Article 2 that relate primarily to the sale-of-goods aspects apply, and the provisions that relate primarily to the transaction as a whole do not apply; (b) if the sale-of-goods aspects predominate, Article 2 applies to the transaction but does not preclude applying other law, in appropriate circumstances, to aspects that do not relate to the sale of goods.

Article 2 does not (a) apply to a transaction that, even though in the form of an unconditional contract to sell or present sale, operates only to create a security interest; or (b) impair or repeal a statute regulating sales to consumers, farmers, or other specified classes of buyers.
c: Article 2 leaves the law of purchase-money security (conditional sales, chattel mortgages) largely to Article 9, though it still governs the sales aspects. A transaction that looks like a sale but creates a security interest is not governed by Article 2 in that respect. See §§ 1-201(b)(35), 9-109(a)(1).

Many deals mix goods with services, leases of other goods, or other property. Before 2022, courts used (i) the "predominant purpose" test (all of Article 2 or none of it), (ii) the "gravamen of the claim" test, or (iii) a "bifurcation" approach (Article 2 for the goods-related provisions only). Subsection (2) codifies a two-tier blend: if goods predominate, Article 2 applies; if not, the goods-related provisions still apply - so the person acquiring goods still gets warranty protection and may be a buyer in ordinary course.

The test asks which aspect predominates, not the parties' "purpose" (though purpose may be a factor). The court decides case by case with no fixed formula. Factors: the language of the agreement; the share of the total price attributable to goods (an agreed allocation ordinarily binds the parties); the parties' purposes, if ascertainable; and the nature of the parties' businesses (for example, whether the seller is in the business of selling such goods). Services in manufacturing specially manufactured goods normally count toward the goods side; design services normally do not.

Even when goods predominate, principles of law and equity still supplement Article 2 (§ 1-103(b)), and other law may govern the non-goods aspects, depending on that law's purpose and whether it would interfere with Article 2. Examples: a roofing job (shingles plus installation) can be governed by Article 2 while a roofer-licensing or cancellation statute still applies to the services; in a sale of a warehouse full of goods together with the building and land, real property law governs the land.

If goods do not predominate, the goods-related provisions apply: warranties (§§ 2-312 to 2-318), tender and risk of loss (§§ 2-503, 2-504, 2-509, 2-510), acceptance, rejection, and cure (§§ 2-508, 2-601 to 2-606), and buyer's remedies for nondelivery or nonconforming goods (§§ 2-711 to 2-716). Provisions on the transaction as a whole do not apply: the signed-record requirement (§ 2-201), formation (§§ 2-204 to 2-207), and modification without consideration (§ 2-209). Examples: in a services-predominant roofing deal, formation by purchase order and confirmation is governed by other law; excuse for a late finish is governed by general contract law, not § 2-615; the parol evidence rule of § 2-202 applies only to evidence about the goods. In a kitchen remodel where services predominate, Article 2 still decides whether the owner can reject a nonconforming oven, cover, and recover damages for it - but not damages for finishing the project late.

Subsections (1) and (2) are gap fillers. Parties may agree that Article 2 will not govern non-goods aspects even when goods predominate (for example, the services part of a design-build-sell robotics deal). But when goods predominate they cannot opt out of Article 2 for matters that concern the transaction as a whole, such as formation and the statute of frauds. Article 2's provisions may otherwise be varied as § 1-302 allows.

statutes.t: Definitions and Index of Definitions
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 1 - Short Title, General Construction and Subject Matter
x: In Article 2, unless the context otherwise requires: (a) "Buyer" means a person who buys or contracts to buy goods; (b) [Reserved - the old merchant-only "good faith" definition was deleted; § 1-201(b)(20) now applies to everyone]; (c) "Receipt" of goods means taking physical possession of them; (d) "Seller" means a person who sells or contracts to sell goods.

Index of other Article 2 definitions, including: "Acceptance" § 2-606; "Between merchants" § 2-104; "Cancellation" § 2-106(4); "Commercial unit" § 2-105; "Conforming to contract" § 2-106; "Contract for sale" § 2-106; "Cover" § 2-712; "Entrusting" § 2-403; "Future goods" § 2-105; "Goods" § 2-105; "Identification" § 2-501; "Installment contract" § 2-612; "Lot" § 2-105; "Merchant" § 2-104; "Present sale" § 2-106; "Sale" § 2-106; "Sale on approval" and "Sale or return" § 2-326; "Termination" § 2-106.
Definitions from other articles also apply, such as "Check" and "Draft" (§ 3-104), "Consignee" and "Consignor" (§ 7-102), "Consumer goods" (§ 9-102), and "Dishonor" (§ 3-502).
Article 1's general definitions and principles of construction apply throughout Article 2.
c: "Any legal successor in interest" was dropped from "buyer" and "seller" because § 2-210 limits some delegations, so not every successor can safely be included - though in the ordinary case successors are included.

"Receipt" (physical possession) must be distinguished from "delivery": a seller may fulfill its obligation to deliver (for example, by shipment) even though the buyer never receives the goods. This distinction drives the risk-of-loss rule in § 2-509(3).

statutes.t: Definitions: "Merchant"; "Between Merchants"; "Financing Agency"
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 1 - Short Title, General Construction and Subject Matter
x: "Merchant" means a person who (i) deals in goods of the kind, or (ii) otherwise by occupation holds itself out as having knowledge or skill peculiar to the practices or goods involved in the transaction, or (iii) to whom such knowledge or skill may be attributed because it employs an agent, broker, or other intermediary who by occupation holds itself out as having such knowledge or skill.

"Financing agency" means a bank, finance company, or other person who in the ordinary course of business makes advances against goods or documents of title, or who by arrangement with the seller or buyer intervenes in ordinary course to make or collect payment under the contract (for example, by purchasing or paying the seller's draft).
"Between merchants" means any transaction in which both parties are chargeable with the knowledge or skill of merchants.
c: Article 2 assumes that dealings between professionals need special, clear rules that may not suit a casual or inexperienced buyer or seller, so it states rules "between merchants" and "as against a merchant" expressly. This section defines who the professionals are.

Merchant status may rest on specialized knowledge of the goods, of business practices, or both; which kind is enough depends on the provision. Three groups: (1) §§ 2-201(2), 2-205, 2-207, and 2-209 (statute of frauds confirmations, firm offers, confirmations and battle of the forms, modification) rest on ordinary business practices such as answering mail, so almost any person in business - even a bank or university - is a merchant for these, but only when acting in a mercantile capacity (a lawyer buying fishing tackle for personal use is not). (2) § 2-314 (merchantability) applies only if the seller is a merchant "with respect to goods of that kind" - a much narrower group; § 2-402(2) and § 2-403(2) (entrusting to a merchant who "deals in goods of that kind") are in the same class. (3) §§ 2-327(1)(c), 2-603, 2-605 (merchant buyer's duties), 2-509 (risk of loss), and 2-609 (adequate assurance) apply to merchants under either the practices or the goods test.
Through the agent or broker clause, even a university can be a merchant if it has a regular purchasing department or business staff familiar with business practices.
k: deals in goods of the kind

statutes.t: Definitions: Transferability; "Goods"; "Future" Goods; "Lot"; "Commercial Unit"
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 1 - Short Title, General Construction and Subject Matter
x: "Goods" means all things (including specially manufactured goods) which are movable at the time of identification to the contract for sale, other than the money in which the price is to be paid, investment securities (Article 8), and things in action. "Goods" also includes the unborn young of animals, growing crops, and other identified things attached to realty as described in § 2-107.

Goods must be both existing and identified before any interest in them can pass. Goods that are not both existing and identified are "future" goods. A purported present sale of future goods operates as a contract to sell.
There may be a sale of a part interest in existing identified goods.

An undivided share in an identified bulk of fungible goods is sufficiently identified to be sold even though the quantity of the bulk is not determined; a buyer of an agreed proportion or quantity becomes an owner in common, to the extent of the seller's interest.
"Lot" means a parcel or single article that is the subject of a separate sale or delivery, whether or not it is enough to perform the contract.

"Commercial unit" means a unit of goods that by commercial usage is a single whole for purposes of sale, and division of which materially impairs its character or value on the market or in use - for example, a machine, a suite of furniture or an assortment of sizes, or a bale, gross, or carload.
c: The definition turns on movability; it does not reach things not fairly identifiable as movables before performance. Growing crops (including fruit, perennial hay, nursery stock) and the unborn young of animals are included because they are often sold in advance; a wool crop is too. Excluding "money in which the price is to be paid" does not stop money from being goods when it is treated as a commodity (for example, foreign or rare coins). Timber, minerals, and structures are handled by § 2-107. "Fixtures" is avoided; things attached to realty are goods if capable of severance without material harm. Investment securities are excluded, but Article 2 may apply by analogy where sensible.
Contracts for future or contingent goods and co-ownership after sale of a part interest are so obvious they need no express statement; no negative inference should be drawn.
Subsection (4) does not decide when appropriating part of a fungible bulk satisfies the contract.
"Lot" and "commercial unit" are defined to help phrase later sections (for example, acceptance of a commercial unit under §§ 2-601 and 2-606).
When identification occurs is governed by § 2-501; this section only says what kinds of goods can be sold.

statutes.t: Definitions: "Contract"; "Agreement"; "Contract for Sale"; "Sale"; "Conforming"; "Termination"; "Cancellation"; "Hybrid Transaction"
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 1 - Short Title, General Construction and Subject Matter
x: In Article 2, "contract" and "agreement" are limited to those relating to the present or future sale of goods. "Contract for sale" includes both a present sale and a contract to sell goods at a future time. A "sale" is the passing of title from the seller to the buyer for a price (§ 2-401). A "present sale" is a sale accomplished by the making of the contract.
Goods or conduct, including any part of a performance, are "conforming" when they are in accordance with the obligations under the contract.

"Termination" occurs when either party, under a power created by agreement or law, puts an end to the contract otherwise than for its breach. On termination, all obligations still executory on both sides are discharged, but any right based on prior breach or performance survives.

"Cancellation" occurs when either party puts an end to the contract for breach by the other. Its effect is the same as termination, except that the cancelling party also retains any remedy for breach of the whole contract or any unperformed balance.
"Hybrid transaction" means a single transaction involving a sale of goods and (a) the provision of services; (b) a lease of other goods; or (c) a sale, lease, or license of property other than goods.
c: The parties' rights do not differ between a present sale and a contract to sell unless Article 2 expressly says so.

Subsection (2) continues the policy of requiring exact performance by the seller as a condition of requiring acceptance (the perfect tender idea). The seller is protected from sudden buyer technicality by the cure rule of § 2-508, and usage of trade, course of dealing, and course of performance often allow commercial leeway in what counts as conforming.
Termination and cancellation are kept distinct throughout Article 2.

When the passing of title for a price is part of a larger deal (services, a lease of other goods, rights in other property), the deal is a "hybrid transaction"; § 2-102 says how far Article 2 applies.

A hybrid is a single transaction. Separate agreements made at the same time are evaluated separately (a business sale split into a goods contract, a consulting contract, and an intangibles contract has no hybrid). Even one agreement may contain independent, severable transactions - a farmer's sale of a tractor at a set price plus a separately priced promise to board cattle is two transactions, and Article 2 governs only the tractor. But a landscaper's single price for selling and installing plants, with no allocation, is a hybrid.

statutes.t: Goods to Be Severed from Realty: Recording
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 1 - Short Title, General Construction and Subject Matter
x: A contract for the sale of minerals or the like (including oil and gas), or a structure or its materials, to be removed from realty is a contract for the sale of goods if they are to be severed by the seller. Until severance, a purported present sale that is not effective as a transfer of an interest in land is effective only as a contract to sell.

A contract for the sale apart from the land of growing crops, other things attached to realty and capable of severance without material harm (not covered by (1)), or timber to be cut is a contract for the sale of goods whether the buyer or the seller is to sever them, even though they are part of the realty at contracting; the parties can by identification make a present sale before severance.

These rules are subject to third-party rights under realty-records law; the contract may be executed and recorded as a document transferring an interest in land, and recording then gives third parties notice of the buyer's rights.
c: Subsection (1) applies only if the minerals or structures are to be severed by the seller. If the buyer is to sever them, the deal is a contract affecting land, governed by the land statute of frauds and recording law rather than § 2-201.

Under (2), things attached to realty that can be severed without material harm are goods no matter who severs them. "Fixtures" is avoided in favor of the "severance without material harm" test. Recording under (3) preserves the buyer's rights.

Security interests in things attached to realty are governed by Article 9, whose definition of goods differs; both articles treat growing crops and timber to be cut under a severance contract as goods.

statutes.t: Formal Requirements; Statute of Frauds
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 2 - Form, Formation and Readjustment of Contract
x: Except as otherwise provided in this section, a contract for the sale of goods for the price of $500 or more is not enforceable by way of action or defense unless there is a record sufficient to indicate that a contract for sale has been made between the parties and signed by the party against whom enforcement is sought or by its authorized agent or broker. A record is not insufficient because it omits or incorrectly states a term agreed upon, but the contract is not enforceable under this subsection beyond the quantity of goods shown in the record.

Between merchants, if within a reasonable time a record in confirmation of the contract and sufficient against the sender is received, and the party receiving it has reason to know its contents, it satisfies (1) against the recipient unless notice in a record of objection to its contents is given within 10 days after it is received.

A contract that does not satisfy (1) but is valid in other respects is enforceable: (a) if the goods are to be specially manufactured for the buyer and are not suitable for sale to others in the ordinary course of the seller's business, and the seller, before notice of repudiation is received and under circumstances which reasonably indicate that the goods are for the buyer, has made either a substantial beginning of their manufacture or commitments for their procurement; (b) if the party against whom enforcement is sought admits in its pleading, testimony, or otherwise in court that a contract for sale was made - but not beyond the quantity of goods admitted; or (c) with respect to goods for which payment has been made and accepted or which have been received and accepted (§ 2-606).
c: The record need not contain all material terms, and those stated need not be precise; it need only give a basis for believing the oral evidence rests on a real transaction. Pencil on a scratch pad is enough, and it need not say who is buyer and who is seller. Price, time and place of payment or delivery, quality, and warranties may all be omitted (price can be supplied as a reasonable price, from a known price list, or from market prices). The only term that must appear is quantity - it need not be accurate, but recovery is limited to the amount stated. Three invariable requirements: the record must (1) evidence a contract for the sale of goods, (2) be "signed" (any authentication identifying the party to be charged), and (3) specify a quantity.

Part performance validates the contract only for goods accepted or for which payment was made and accepted. Receipt and acceptance of goods or price is an unambiguous admission that a contract exists, so the court may apportion: the price of delivered goods can be recovered, or a buyer who paid can compel delivery of an apportionable part. Part payment may be by money or check accepted by the seller; if the price is goods or services, they must be delivered and accepted.

Between merchants, failing to answer a confirming record within ten days of receipt is treated as a signed record and makes it sufficient against both parties. Its only effect is to remove the statute of frauds defense from the party who failed to answer; the party relying on the confirmation still bears the burden of persuading the trier of fact that an oral contract was actually made. Compare the effect of silence under § 2-207.

Failing the statute does not make the contract void for all purposes; it only prevents judicial enforcement by a party. A buyer who takes possession under an unrepudiated oral contract is not a trespasser, and a third party who wrongfully induces a breach cannot use the statute as a defense.
For what counts as "signing," see § 1-201, Comment 37.

For (1), the record need not be delivered to anyone and need not be signed by both parties - but it is not sufficient against a party who has not signed. From contracting on, each party should realize that the other's signature is the one that matters to it.

If the contract is admitted in court - in a pleading, a stipulation, or oral statement - no record is needed, and a party cannot admit the contract yet still claim the statute as a defense. The admission is evidence against the admitting party of the facts admitted and nothing more, and it is no evidence against the other party.
For medium neutrality, "writing" became "record" in 2022.

statutes.t: Final Written Expression: Parol or Extrinsic Evidence
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 2 - Form, Formation and Readjustment of Contract
x: Terms on which the parties' confirmatory memoranda agree, or which are otherwise set forth in a record intended by the parties as a final expression of their agreement with respect to the terms included, may not be contradicted by evidence of any prior agreement or of a contemporaneous oral agreement, but may be explained or supplemented:
by course of performance, course of dealing, or usage of trade (§ 1-303); and
by evidence of consistent additional terms, unless the court finds the record to have been intended also as a complete and exclusive statement of the terms of the agreement.
c: The section rejects (a) any assumption that because a record is final on some matters it includes all matters agreed; (b) the premise that language means what legal rules of construction say rather than what it means in its commercial context; and (c) any requirement that the court first find the language ambiguous before admitting course of dealing, usage of trade, or course of performance.

Course of dealing, usage of trade, and course of performance are admissible to explain or supplement any record, so that the parties' true understanding is reached. Records are read assuming those practices were taken for granted when drafted; unless carefully negated, they become part of the meaning of the words. Course of actual performance is the best indication of what the parties meant the record to say.

Consistent additional terms not in the record may be proved unless the court finds both parties intended the record as a complete and exclusive statement of all terms. If the additional terms, had they been agreed, would certainly have been included in the record in the court's view, evidence of them must be kept from the trier of fact.
For medium neutrality, "writing" became "record" in 2022.

statutes.t: Formation in General
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 2 - Form, Formation and Readjustment of Contract
x: A contract for sale of goods may be made in any manner sufficient to show agreement, including conduct by both parties which recognizes the existence of such a contract.
An agreement sufficient to constitute a contract for sale may be found even though the moment of its making is undetermined.

Even though one or more terms are left open, a contract for sale does not fail for indefiniteness if the parties have intended to make a contract and there is a reasonably certain basis for giving an appropriate remedy.
c: Any manner of expressing agreement - oral, written, or conduct - can form a contract, subject to the rest of Article 2. Subsection (2) covers cases where the correspondence does not show exactly when the deal closed but the parties' actions show a binding obligation. Subsection (3) is the "open terms" principle behind Part 3: if the parties intend to be bound, missing terms do not defeat the contract if there is any reasonably certain basis for a remedy. The test is not certainty about what each party was to do or the exact damages, and leaving terms to be agreed later does not by itself defeat the deal; commercial standards of indefiniteness apply, and the Code supplies missing terms elsewhere. The more terms left open, the less likely the parties intended to be bound - but their conduct may settle the question.

statutes.t: Firm Offers
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 2 - Form, Formation and Readjustment of Contract
x: An offer by a merchant to buy or sell goods in a signed record which by its terms gives assurance that it will be held open is not revocable, for lack of consideration, during the time stated or, if no time is stated, for a reasonable time - but in no event may the period of irrevocability exceed three months. Any such term of assurance on a form supplied by the offeree must be separately signed by the offeror.
c: The section drops the old rule that a firm offer needs consideration; it need only be stated as firm and made in a signed record.

The aim is to honor a merchant's deliberate intention to make a current offer binding. Deliberateness is shown by the merchant's signature on an individualized document, or by separately signing the clause on a form supplied by the other party (typically at least initialing it). A handwritten memo on letterhead "confirming" a firm offer may suffice even without a subscription, and so may an authorized telegram. But an oral firm offer stays revocable even if course of dealing or trade usage treats such offers as binding - a signed record is the essence of the section.

The section covers current firm offers, not long-term options, so it caps irrevocability at three months. The period need not be stated in days; an offer "firm" until an event within three months stays open until that event. A longer promise binds only for the first three months (but may be renewed). An offer supported by consideration is an option and can last as long as agreed; this section deals only with offers lacking consideration.

Requiring separate signing protects an offeror from inadvertently signing a firm-offer clause buried in the offeree's form. If the clause is called to the offeror's attention and separately signed, it binds; § 2-302 can still prevent unconscionable results from other terms on the form.
Good faith and the general law of mistake give relief for a material mistake.
For medium neutrality, "writing" became "record" in 2022.

statutes.t: Offer and Acceptance in Formation of Contract
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 2 - Form, Formation and Readjustment of Contract
x: Unless otherwise unambiguously indicated by the language or circumstances: (a) an offer to make a contract shall be construed as inviting acceptance in any manner and by any medium reasonable in the circumstances; (b) an order or other offer to buy goods for prompt or current shipment shall be construed as inviting acceptance either by a prompt promise to ship or by the prompt or current shipment of conforming or nonconforming goods - but a shipment of nonconforming goods is not an acceptance if the seller seasonably notifies the buyer that the shipment is offered only as an accommodation to the buyer.

Where the beginning of a requested performance is a reasonable mode of acceptance, an offeror who is not notified of acceptance within a reasonable time may treat the offer as having lapsed before acceptance.
c: Any reasonable manner of acceptance is available unless the offeror has made quite clear it is not. Old technical rules (a telegraphed offer must be accepted by telegram) are rejected, and the rule should flex as new media develop.

An order for current shipment can be accepted by shipping or by a prompt promise to ship, even if it says "ship at once"; the section rejects the idea that an offer normally contemplates a single mode of acceptance. "Shipment" has its § 2-504 meaning and does not include starting delivery in the seller's own truck - though loading the seller's truck might be a beginning of performance under (2).

Beginning performance binds the offeror only if followed within a reasonable time by notice to the offeror, and the beginning must unambiguously show the offeree's intent to be bound. Common law may still let a begun performance temporarily bar revocation or, at the offeror's option, count as acceptance.

A shipment of nonconforming goods made in response to an order is normally understood to close the deal even though it is also a breach (an acceptance and a breach at once). The seller avoids that result by notifying the buyer that the shipment is nonconforming and offered only as an accommodation - then it is a counteroffer, not an acceptance.

statutes.t: Additional Terms in Acceptance or Confirmation
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 2 - Form, Formation and Readjustment of Contract
x: A definite and seasonable expression of acceptance or a written confirmation sent within a reasonable time operates as an acceptance even though it states terms additional to or different from those offered or agreed upon, unless acceptance is expressly made conditional on assent to the additional or different terms.

The additional terms are to be construed as proposals for addition to the contract. Between merchants, such terms become part of the contract unless: (a) the offer expressly limits acceptance to the terms of the offer; (b) they materially alter it; or (c) notification of objection to them has already been given or is given within a reasonable time after notice of them is received.

Conduct by both parties which recognizes the existence of a contract is sufficient to establish a contract for sale although the writings of the parties do not otherwise establish a contract. In that case, the terms of the contract consist of the terms on which the writings of the parties agree, together with any supplementary terms incorporated under any other provisions of the UCC.
c: Two typical situations: (i) a written confirmation sent after an oral or informal agreement that adds terms not discussed; and (ii) an offer and acceptance where the acceptance adds minor proposals ("ship by Tuesday," "rush"). A frequent example of (ii) is the exchange of a printed purchase order and an acknowledgment form whose terms do not match - and the parties go ahead anyway.

A deal that in commercial understanding has been closed is a contract (rejecting the mirror image rule). Additional matter in the confirmation or acceptance is a proposal under (2) unless the acceptance is made expressly conditional on assent to it.

Whether added terms join the contract depends on (2). Terms that materially alter the bargain come in only if the other party expressly agrees; terms that do not are incorporated unless objection is given in advance or within a reasonable time.

Clauses that normally "materially alter" the contract because they would cause surprise or hardship if incorporated without express awareness: negating standard warranties such as merchantability or fitness where they normally attach; requiring a 90% or 100% delivery guaranty where trade usage allows more quantity leeway (for example, a cannery); reserving the seller's power to cancel if the buyer misses any invoice when due; requiring complaints in a time materially shorter than customary or reasonable.

Clauses with no unreasonable surprise that come in unless seasonably objected to: stating or slightly enlarging the seller's excuse for supervening causes beyond its control (like § 2-615) or a reasonable proration formula; a reasonable time for complaints within customary limits, or inspection by a sub-purchaser; interest on overdue invoices or the seller's standard credit terms within trade practice; limiting rejection for defects within customary trade tolerances or otherwise limiting remedy in a reasonable manner (see §§ 2-718, 2-719).

If no answer comes within a reasonable time, it is fair to assume assent to the added terms. Where clauses on the parties' confirming forms conflict, each party is assumed to object to the other's conflicting clause, so the notice-of-objection requirement is met and the conflicting terms drop out (the knockout idea). The contract then consists of the terms expressly agreed, terms on which the confirmations agree, and terms supplied by the Code, including (2). A confirmation is also subject to § 2-201: there silence permits enforcement of a prior oral deal; here silence lets additional terms in.

Often, as when goods are shipped, accepted, and paid for before any dispute, there is no doubt a contract exists. Where the writings do not establish one, there is no need to decide which document was the offer and which the acceptance (see § 2-204); the only question is the terms, and (3) governs.

The 2022 amendments changed "writing" to "record" in some sections (such as §§ 2-201 and 2-202) but not this one. Where "writing" remains, electronic records may still be given effect under other law such as E-SIGN and UETA.

statutes.t: [Deleted] Course of Performance or Practical Construction
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 2 - Form, Formation and Readjustment of Contract
x: No text. See § 1-303(a) (definition of course of performance), § 1-303(d)-(e) (its use and its rank in the hierarchy), and § 1-303(f) (course of performance can show waiver or modification, subject to § 2-209).
c: Former cmt. 4

Cited in the outline: a single occasion of conduct does not create a course of performance. Course of performance requires repeated occasions for performance accepted or acquiesced in without objection, which is now the test in § 1-303(a).
statutes.note: Deleted and moved to § 1-303 (course of performance now sits with course of dealing and usage of trade). The 2026 supplement prints only "[Deleted]." Class slides and the outline still cite § 2-208.

statutes.t: Modification, Rescission and Waiver
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 2 - Form, Formation and Readjustment of Contract
x: An agreement modifying a contract within Article 2 needs no consideration to be binding.

A signed agreement which excludes modification or rescission except by a signed writing or other signed record cannot be otherwise modified or rescinded, but except as between merchants such a requirement on a form supplied by the merchant must be separately signed by the other party.
The requirements of the statute of frauds (§ 2-201) must be satisfied if the contract as modified is within its provisions.
Although an attempt at modification or rescission does not satisfy (2) or (3), it can operate as a waiver.

A party who has made a waiver affecting an executory portion of the contract may retract the waiver by reasonable notification received by the other party that strict performance will be required of any term waived, unless the retraction would be unjust in view of a material change of position in reliance on the waiver.
c: The section aims to make all necessary and desirable modifications effective without the technicalities that hampered them.

No consideration is needed, but modifications must meet the good faith test. Using bad faith to escape the original terms, or extorting a "modification" without legitimate commercial reason, is ineffective; a mere technical consideration cannot save a bad faith modification. Good faith includes reasonable commercial standards of fair dealing and may require an objectively demonstrable reason for seeking the change - but a market shift that makes performance a loss can be such a reason even though it would not excuse performance under §§ 2-615 or 2-616.

Subsections (2) and (3) guard against false claims of oral modification. "Modification or rescission" includes abandonment or other change by mutual consent, but not unilateral termination or cancellation (§ 2-106). The statute of frauds applies to modifications; the delivery-and-acceptance exception reaches only goods already accepted (the past), so a future modification at $500 or more cannot be proved by oral testimony alone, and a memo is limited to the quantity stated. Subsection (2) lets the parties write their own statute of frauds (a no-oral-modification clause); a consumer is bound by one on a merchant's form only if the consumer separately signs it.
Subsection (4) keeps a no-oral-modification clause from wiping out the legal effect of the parties' actual later conduct: that conduct can still be a waiver, as regulated by (5).
For medium neutrality, "signed writing" was supplemented with "signed record" in 2022.

statutes.t: Delegation of Performance; Assignment of Rights
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 2 - Form, Formation and Readjustment of Contract
x: A party may perform its duty through a delegate unless otherwise agreed or unless the other party has a substantial interest in having its original promisor perform or control the acts required by the contract. No delegation of performance relieves the delegating party of any duty to perform or any liability for breach.

Except as provided in § 9-406, unless otherwise agreed, all rights of either seller or buyer can be assigned except where the assignment would materially change the duty of the other party, or increase materially the burden or risk imposed on it by its contract, or impair materially its chance of obtaining return performance. A right to damages for breach of the whole contract, or a right arising out of the assignor's due performance of its entire obligation, can be assigned despite agreement otherwise.

Creating, attaching, perfecting, or enforcing a security interest in the seller's interest under a contract is not a transfer that materially changes the buyer's duty, burden, or risk, or impairs its chance of return performance, unless (and only to the extent that) enforcement actually results in a delegation of material performance of the seller. Even then the security interest stays effective, but (i) the seller is liable for damages from the delegation that the buyer could not reasonably prevent, and (ii) a court may grant other relief, including cancellation or an injunction against enforcement.
Unless the circumstances indicate the contrary, a prohibition of assignment of "the contract" is to be construed as barring only the delegation to the assignee of the assignor's performance.

An assignment of "the contract" or of "all my rights under the contract" or similar general terms is an assignment of rights and, unless the language or circumstances (as in an assignment for security) indicate the contrary, a delegation of the assignor's duties; the assignee's acceptance is a promise to perform those duties, enforceable by the assignor or the other original party.

The other party may treat any assignment that delegates performance as creating reasonable grounds for insecurity and may, without prejudice to its rights against the assignor, demand assurances from the assignee (§ 2-609).
c: Delegation of performance and assignment of rights are normal, permitted incidents of a sales contract.
Delegation is allowed where no substantial reason shows the delegated performance will be less satisfactory than personal performance.

Rights that are no longer executory, such as a right to damages for breach, may be assigned despite a prohibition, since no delegation is involved. Subsection (2) is subject to § 9-406, which makes rights to payment for goods sold ("accounts"), earned or not, freely assignable notwithstanding a contrary agreement or rule of law.

The nature of the contract may bar assignment even without delegation - an issue in output, requirements, and exclusive-dealing contracts. Section 2-306 removes most of the "personal discretion" element by substituting a good-faith standard of operating the business, and § 2-609 lets the other party demand adequate assurance and suspend performance meanwhile. "Performance" includes giving orders under a requirements contract. Where a material personal discretion would be transferred, assignment is barred by (2).

Subsection (4) is a rule of construction distinguishing a normal commercial assignment (assignee substitutes for assignor as to rights and duties) from a financing assignment (only rights pass). Whether the original parties can still readjust the contract after a financing assignment is left to Article 9.
The non-assigning party has a stake in the reliability of the person it contracted with, so it is entitled to assurance that delegated performance will be forthcoming.
The section is not a complete law of assignment and delegation; it does not address notice of assignment, rights of successive assignees, or form of assignment. Some of these are in Article 9.

statutes.t: General Obligations of Parties
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 3 - General Obligation and Construction of Contract
x: The obligation of the seller is to transfer and deliver, and that of the buyer is to accept and pay, in accordance with the contract.
c: "Obligation" (rather than "duty") is used so that delivery and payment also work as conditions, except as other sections (such as cure) modify them. What is "in accordance with the contract" is judged by usage of trade, course of dealing and performance, and the surrounding circumstances, together with the ordinary meaning of the words.

statutes.t: Unconscionable Contract or Clause
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 3 - General Obligation and Construction of Contract
x: If the court as a matter of law finds the contract or any clause to have been unconscionable at the time it was made, the court may refuse to enforce the contract, or enforce the remainder without the unconscionable clause, or so limit the application of any unconscionable clause as to avoid any unconscionable result.

When it is claimed or appears to the court that the contract or any clause may be unconscionable, the parties shall be afforded a reasonable opportunity to present evidence as to its commercial setting, purpose, and effect to aid the court's determination.
c: Courts once policed unfair terms indirectly - by adverse construction, by manipulating offer and acceptance, or by public policy. This section lets the court rule directly, as a conclusion of law. The basic test is whether, in light of the general commercial background and the commercial needs of the particular trade or case, the clauses are so one-sided as to be unconscionable under the circumstances at the time of contracting. The principle is the prevention of oppression and unfair surprise (cf. Campbell Soup Co. v. Wentz), not disturbance of the allocation of risks because of superior bargaining power. The comment lists older cases that reached fair results by narrow readings: a complaint-time limit not applied to latent defects found only by microscope; a disclaimer read to cover only express warranties; a description obligation surviving a disclaimer when a used car was delivered as "new"; a no-rejection clause limited to mere mercantile variations; and a "with all faults" clause not overriding the warranty of description.

The court may refuse to enforce a contract permeated by unconscionability, strike a clause or group of clauses so tainted or contrary to the essential purpose of the agreement, or limit a clause to avoid unconscionable results.
The question is for the court, not the jury; the commercial evidence under (2) is for the court. Only the agreement as the court shapes it goes to the trier of fact.

statutes.t: Price Payable in Money, Goods, Realty, or Otherwise
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 3 - General Obligation and Construction of Contract
x: The price can be made payable in money or otherwise. If it is payable in whole or in part in goods, each party is a seller of the goods it is to transfer.

Even though all or part of the price is payable in an interest in realty, the transfer of the goods and the seller's obligations as to them are subject to Article 2, but not the transfer of the interest in realty or the transferor's obligations in connection with it.
c: The section corrects old Sales Act phrasing and rejects purely verbal constructions that ignore the provision's purpose.

Article 2 applies when the price is something other than money (a barter), but that does not mean every provision applies automatically just because the transfer is not a gift; each provision's purposes must be considered.
When goods are exchanged for realty, Article 2 governs only the goods side, not the land transfer, which is left to other law; local realty statutes are not lightly displaced.

statutes.t: Open Price Term
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 3 - General Obligation and Construction of Contract
x: The parties, if they so intend, can conclude a contract for sale even though the price is not settled. The price is then a reasonable price at the time for delivery if (a) nothing is said as to price; (b) the price is left to be agreed by the parties and they fail to agree; or (c) the price is to be fixed by some agreed market or other standard as set or recorded by a third person or agency and it is not so set or recorded.
A price to be fixed by the seller or by the buyer means a price for that party to fix in good faith.

When a price to be fixed otherwise than by agreement of the parties fails to be fixed through the fault of one party, the other may at its option treat the contract as cancelled or itself fix a reasonable price.

Where the parties intend not to be bound unless the price is fixed or agreed, and it is not, there is no contract. The buyer must return any goods received or, if unable, pay their reasonable value at the time of delivery, and the seller must return any part of the price paid on account.
c: When the parties intend to be bound, Article 2 rejects the formula that "an agreement to agree is unenforceable" and rejects defeating the deal for indefiniteness. Because remedies like cover (§ 2-712), resale (§ 2-706), and specific performance (§ 2-716) do not depend on exact contract-price arithmetic, there is usually a "reasonably certain basis" for a remedy.
Sometimes postponing agreement on price means no deal was concluded - hence "if they so intend" and subsection (4). In most cases that is a question for the trier of fact.

A price to be fixed by one party must be fixed in good faith, which includes reasonable commercial standards of fair dealing; the seller cannot charge any price it wishes. In the normal case a posted price, "price in effect," "market price," or the like satisfies good faith.

Sometimes a named person's judgment is not just a barometer of fair price but an essential condition of the deal. A trusted expert's valuation of a unique painting with no market differs from an expert's grading of cotton; if the expert is unavailable, the first may mean no contract, the second still a contract.

Under (3), wrongful interference with agreed price-fixing machinery may be treated as a repudiation justifying cancellation, or as a failure to cooperate that shifts the leeway in fixing the price to the aggrieved party.
The aim is to give effect to the deal made, always subject to the good faith required of all contracts (§ 1-304).

statutes.t: Output, Requirements and Exclusive Dealings
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 3 - General Obligation and Construction of Contract
x: A term which measures the quantity by the output of the seller or the requirements of the buyer means such actual output or requirements as may occur in good faith, except that no quantity unreasonably disproportionate to any stated estimate or, in the absence of a stated estimate, to any normal or otherwise comparable prior output or requirements may be tendered or demanded.

A lawful agreement by either the seller or the buyer for exclusive dealing in the kind of goods concerned imposes, unless otherwise agreed, an obligation by the seller to use best efforts to supply the goods and by the buyer to use best efforts to promote their sale.
c: Subsection (1) reads commercial background and intent into output and requirements terms and demands good faith; it applies to dealers and distributors as well as manufacturers.

Such contracts are not too indefinite (they mean actual good faith output or requirements) and do not lack mutuality, because the party fixing quantity must run its business in good faith and by commercial standards of fair dealing, so the quantity approximates a reasonably foreseeable figure. Reasonable elasticity is expected, and good faith variations are allowed even to the point of discontinuance: a requirements buyer's shutdown for lack of orders may be permissible when a shutdown merely to curtail losses would not. The essential test is good faith. A sudden plant expansion is not covered, but normal good faith expansion is; a sharp rise in market price under a fixed-price requirements contract is a factor.

If the agreement states an estimate, no quantity unreasonably disproportionate to it may be tendered or demanded. Agreed minimums or maximums clearly limit elasticity, and the estimate is the center around which variation is expected.

Whether the buyer of a business is bound by an existing output or requirements contract is for other law. If the contract continues, quantity is still measured by good faith normal operation before the sale; the sale itself does not justify a sudden expansion or decrease.

In exclusive dealing, the parties impliedly bind themselves to reasonable diligence as well as good faith: the exclusive agent must use reasonable effort and due diligence to expand the market or promote the product, and the principal must not supply other dealers in the exclusive territory. Exclusive dealing raises the same good faith issues as (1) and can raise insecurity and adequate assurance questions.

statutes.t: Delivery in Single Lot or Several Lots
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 3 - General Obligation and Construction of Contract
x: Unless otherwise agreed, all goods called for by a contract for sale must be tendered in a single delivery, and payment is due only on such tender; but where the circumstances give either party the right to make or demand delivery in lots, the price, if it can be apportioned, may be demanded for each lot.
c: Absent agreement, the parties are presumed to intend delivery in a single lot.
Unless the agreement or circumstances indicate otherwise, delivery in lots is not permitted, and the buyer may reject a deficient tender, subject to the seller's right to cure.

The "but" clause covers cases where a single delivery is not commercially feasible: ten carloads of coal when only three cars are available; brick for a building when the buyer lacks storage space; cattle that must be gathered from the range; goods that must be mined. There a partial delivery cannot be rejected for quantity alone unless the circumstances show repudiation or default as to the balance, or give grounds for insecurity under § 2-609. The balance must still come within a reasonable time and manner (§ 2-503), and § 2-608 lets the buyer revoke acceptance of a lot accepted on the assumption a defect would be cured if cure does not seasonably occur.
Where a party has a right to delivery in lots, the price may be demanded for each lot if it can be apportioned.

statutes.t: Absence of Specified Place for Delivery
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 3 - General Obligation and Construction of Contract
x: Unless otherwise agreed: (a) the place for delivery of goods is the seller's place of business or, if it has none, its residence; but (b) in a contract for sale of identified goods which to the knowledge of the parties at the time of contracting are in some other place, that place is the place for their delivery; and (c) documents of title may be delivered through customary banking channels.
c: Paragraphs (a) and (b) cover noncommercial sales and occasional commercial sales where no place or means of delivery was agreed. When delivery by carrier is "required or authorized by the agreement," § 2-504 governs the seller's delivery duties instead.

When both parties know the identified goods are somewhere other than the seller's place of business, that place is presumed to be the place of delivery. This also applies to a bulk held by a bailee (unless delivery by documents is intended), but then the seller must also procure the bailee's acknowledgment of the buyer's right to possession.

If customary banking channels only require the bank to notify the buyer that documents are available, tender at the buyer's address is not required; proper use of those channels just keeps the seller from being in default. Article 4, Part 5 and Article 5 govern banks' duties for documentary drafts and letters of credit.
These rules apply only "unless otherwise agreed," and the circumstances, usage of trade, course of dealing, and course of performance can show an "otherwise agreement."

statutes.t: Absence of Specific Time Provisions; Notice of Termination
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 3 - General Obligation and Construction of Contract
x: The time for shipment or delivery or any other action under a contract, if not provided in Article 2 or agreed upon, shall be a reasonable time.
Where the contract provides for successive performances but is indefinite in duration, it is valid for a reasonable time but, unless otherwise agreed, may be terminated at any time by either party.

Termination of a contract by one party, except on the happening of an agreed event, requires that reasonable notification be received by the other party, and an agreement dispensing with notification is invalid if its operation would be unconscionable.
c: Without an agreed time, every action must occur within a reasonable time, judged by good faith and commercial standards (§§ 1-201(b)(20), 1-205, 1-304) - what is acceptable commercial conduct given the nature, purpose, and circumstances of the action. A time implied from circumstances, usage, course of dealing, or course of performance counts as "agreed."
Time of payment, if not agreed, is tied to time of delivery; inspection before payment is covered by § 2-513.
Shipment and delivery facts vary too widely for detailed rules, but surprise is to be avoided, good faith judgment protected, and notice or negotiation favored.
When delivery time is open, an unreasonably early offer or demand for delivery is read as a request, not a final position that itself breaches or puts the other side in breach. See §§ 2-207, 2-609.

Good faith requires reasonable notification before treating a contract as breached because a reasonable time has passed - both where time was always open and where a deadline was waived. When both parties let a reasonable time pass in silence, the reasonable time may be enlarged; the contract may also end by abandonment.

A party need not guess at its peril what a later fact-finder will call reasonable. Communicating a proposed time limit calls for a response, and silence can be acquiescence. If the other party objects, or the demand is just for information, a demand for assurances under § 2-609 is available while negotiating. Only insisting on undue delay or rejecting a reasonable proposal raises flat breach.
Under (2), the reasonable duration depends on the circumstances; where the arrangement has run for years, it can continue indefinitely until notice is given.

Good faith and sound practice call for termination notice that gives the other party reasonable time to find a substitute arrangement. An agreement dispensing with or shortening notice is valid unless its operation would create an unconscionable state of affairs.
Justifiable cancellation for breach is a remedy, not the kind of termination covered here.
No notice is required when the contract ends on an "agreed event" - a term chosen to contrast with an "option" to terminate.

statutes.t: Open Time for Payment or Running of Credit; Authority to Ship Under Reservation
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 3 - General Obligation and Construction of Contract
x: Unless otherwise agreed, payment is due at the time and place at which the buyer is to receive the goods, even though the place of shipment is the place of delivery.

If the seller is authorized to send the goods, it may ship them under reservation and may tender the documents of title, but the buyer may inspect the goods after their arrival before payment is due, unless inspection is inconsistent with the contract (§ 2-513).

If delivery is authorized and made by documents of title other than under (b), payment is due, regardless of where the goods are received, (i) at the time and place the buyer is to receive the tangible documents, or (ii) for electronic documents, at the time the buyer is to receive them and at the seller's place of business (or residence).

Where the seller is required or authorized to ship on credit, the credit period runs from the time of shipment, but post-dating the invoice or delaying its dispatch correspondingly delays the start of the credit period.
c: Payment is due where and when the buyer is to receive the goods, not at the point of delivery (except documentary sales). This preserves the buyer's right to inspect before paying even when risk of loss has already passed or credit has begun running under the delivery term.

The seller is protected too: absent credit, it need not give up possession before payment and may collect by a sight draft against an order bill of lading ("hold until arrival; inspection allowed"). If it ships under reservation, payment is due where and when the buyer is to receive the documents.
Unless otherwise agreed, documents are delivered and paid for in the buyer's city, but payment is due only after the goods arrive, because the buyer need not pay before inspection (§§ 2-512, 2-513).

If goods must be unloaded too fast for inspection on arrival, a seller wanting payment before inspection must put such a term in the contract. But under C.I.F., C.O.D., or cash-against-documents terms payment may be due before inspection.

An agreed credit period runs from shipment or from the invoice date commonly taken as the shipment date; delaying the invoice delays the credit period, since it deprives the buyer of notice of when to pay.

statutes.t: Options and Cooperation Respecting Performance
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 3 - General Obligation and Construction of Contract
x: An agreement for sale that is otherwise sufficiently definite (§ 2-204(3)) is not invalid because it leaves particulars of performance to be specified by one of the parties. Any such specification must be made in good faith and within limits set by commercial reasonableness.

Unless otherwise agreed, specifications relating to assortment of the goods are at the buyer's option and, except as provided in § 2-319(1)(c) and (3), specifications or arrangements relating to shipment are at the seller's option.

Where a specification would materially affect the other party's performance but is not seasonably made, or where one party's cooperation is necessary to the other's agreed performance but is not seasonably forthcoming, the other party, in addition to all other remedies, (a) is excused for any resulting delay in its own performance; and (b) may either proceed to perform in any reasonable manner or, after the time for a material part of its own performance, treat the failure to specify or cooperate as a breach by failure to deliver or accept the goods.
c: Parties may leave details of performance for one of them to fill in without the contract failing for indefiniteness. The specifying party must act in good faith and by commercial standards, so there is no surprise and variation stays within commercial reasonableness. The power to specify may come from course of dealing, usage, or circumstances as well as express words.
Absent other arrangement, assortment is the buyer's option and shipping arrangements are the seller's. The old mechanical test giving the option to the party "first under a duty to move" is rejected.

When a needed option or cooperation is not seasonably forthcoming, the other party's delay is excused and it may proceed in any commercially reasonable manner rather than wait. All other remedies remain, especially the right to demand assurance for insecurity; good faith also allows a request for a reasonable indication of the time and manner of performance.

This remedy does not apply where § 2-614 (substituted performance) governs; there, the other party must offer or demand the substitute performance before claiming rights against the noncooperating party.
