x: Acceptance of goods occurs when the buyer (a) after a reasonable opportunity to inspect the goods signifies to the seller that the goods are conforming or that it will take or retain them in spite of their nonconformity; or (b) fails to make an effective rejection (§ 2-602(1)), but acceptance does not occur until the buyer has had a reasonable opportunity to inspect them; or (c) does any act inconsistent with the seller's ownership - but if the act is wrongful as against the seller, it is an acceptance only if ratified by the seller.
Acceptance of a part of any commercial unit is acceptance of that entire unit.
c: Acceptance means the buyer takes particular goods appropriated to the contract as its own, whether or not obligated to, by words, action, or silence when it is time to speak. For conforming goods, it is just performance of part of the buyer's obligation.
Acceptance is always of identified goods. There is no separate "acceptance of title"; title is immaterial to the parties' rights under Article 2.
Payment after tender is one circumstance tending to show acceptance, but never conclusive by itself. A conditional communication of acceptance remains subject to its conditions.

Any act inconsistent with the buyer's claim of rejection is acceptance under (c), except acts the rejection sections permit (holding, salvage, resale). An acceptance resting on the buyer's own wrongful act binds only at the wronged seller's option. After rejecting, a buyer cannot unilaterally switch to acceptance under (a) unless the seller re-tendered or showed it was holding the tender open.
Partial acceptance is valid but only for whole commercial units.

statutes.t: Effect of Acceptance; Notice of Breach; Burden of Establishing Breach After Acceptance; Notice of Claim or Litigation to Person Answerable Over
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 6 - Breach, Repudiation and Excuse
x: The buyer must pay at the contract rate for any goods accepted.

Acceptance of goods precludes rejection of the goods accepted and, if made with knowledge of a nonconformity, cannot be revoked because of it unless the acceptance was on the reasonable assumption that the nonconformity would be seasonably cured; but acceptance does not of itself impair any other remedy provided by Article 2 for nonconformity.

Where a tender has been accepted: (a) the buyer must within a reasonable time after it discovers or should have discovered any breach notify the seller of breach or be barred from any remedy; and (b) if the claim is for infringement or the like (§ 2-312(3)) and the buyer is sued, it must notify the seller within a reasonable time after receiving notice of the litigation or be barred from any remedy over for liability established by the litigation.
The burden is on the buyer to establish any breach with respect to the goods accepted.

Where the buyer is sued for breach of a warranty or other obligation for which its seller is answerable over: (a) it may give its seller written notice of the litigation; if the notice states that the seller may come in and defend and that, if it does not, it will be bound in any action by its buyer by any determination of fact common to the two litigations, then unless the seller after seasonable receipt comes in and defends, it is so bound (vouching in); (b) for infringement claims, the original seller may demand in writing that its buyer turn over control of the litigation, including settlement, or else be barred from any remedy over, and if it also agrees to bear all expense and satisfy any adverse judgment, a buyer who does not turn over control after seasonable receipt is so barred.
Subsections (3), (4), and (5) apply to any obligation of a buyer to hold the seller harmless against infringement (§ 2-312(3)).
c: Once the buyer accepts, the seller is entitled to the price on the contract terms; for partial acceptance the price is reasonably apportioned at the contract rate.

Acceptance bars later rejection; any return must be by revocation of acceptance under § 2-608. Revocation is not available for a nonconformity the buyer knew of at acceptance, unless it accepted reasonably assuming the defect would be seasonably cured.
All other remedies remain, including full rights as to future installments after accepting a nonconforming earlier one.

Timing of notice is judged by commercial standards for a merchant buyer; for a retail consumer the reasonable time is extended, because the rule targets commercial bad faith, not good faith consumers. The notice need only let the seller know the transaction is still troublesome and must be watched; it need not list all objections (unlike § 2-605), claim damages, or threaten litigation - it just has to inform the seller that a breach is claimed, opening the way to settlement.

Third-party beneficiaries (§ 2-318) are not bound by the acceptance-based notice rule, but must notify the seller that an injury occurred, with the extended time allowed lay consumers, and in good faith once aware of the legal situation.

The buyer bears the burden of proving breach after acceptance; this becomes procedural once a nonconforming tender was accepted and notice given, and the buyer may recover by cross-claim or by recoupment against the price.
(3)(b) and (5)(b) let an infringement warrantor defend or settle third-party claims; (5)(a) codifies vouching in for all warranties.
All of these provisions are subject to explicit reservation of rights.
On records other than writings, see § 2-207, Comment 8.

statutes.t: Revocation of Acceptance in Whole or in Part
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 6 - Breach, Repudiation and Excuse
x: The buyer may revoke its acceptance of a lot or commercial unit whose nonconformity substantially impairs its value to the buyer if it accepted it (a) on the reasonable assumption that its nonconformity would be cured and it has not been seasonably cured; or (b) without discovery of the nonconformity, if its acceptance was reasonably induced either by the difficulty of discovery before acceptance or by the seller's assurances.

Revocation must occur within a reasonable time after the buyer discovers or should have discovered the ground for it and before any substantial change in condition of the goods not caused by their own defects. It is not effective until the buyer notifies the seller.
A buyer who so revokes has the same rights and duties as to the goods as if it had rejected them.
c: The buyer need not elect between revocation and damages; both are available. The term "rescission" is avoided.

Revocation requires that the nonconformity substantially impair the value of the goods to the buyer. The test is not what the seller knew at contracting but whether the defect in fact substantially impairs value to this buyer, even if the seller did not know the buyer's particular circumstances (a subjective-objective test).

Seller "assurances" under (1)(b) may come from the circumstances or contract as well as express words at delivery; they matter because they lead the buyer to delay discovery. Fraud remedies are also available.

Because revocation usually follows failed adjustment attempts, the reasonable time is generally longer than the time to give notice of breach, discover defects, or reject. Parties may limit it by agreement, subject to reasonableness.

The notice's content is judged by good faith, preventing surprise, and reasonable adjustment; usually more than a bare notice of breach is needed, but § 2-605's particularization rules do not apply, and standards are looser for nonmerchant buyers.
A buyer cannot revoke if the goods have materially deteriorated other than from their own defects. Worthless goods need not be offered back, and minor defects in returned items are disregarded.
Partial revocation is allowed for the whole lot or any commercial unit.

statutes.t: Right to Adequate Assurance of Performance
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 6 - Breach, Repudiation and Excuse
x: A contract for sale imposes an obligation on each party that the other's expectation of receiving due performance will not be impaired. When reasonable grounds for insecurity arise with respect to the performance of either party, the other may in writing demand adequate assurance of due performance and, until it receives such assurance, may if commercially reasonable suspend any performance for which it has not already received the agreed return.
Between merchants, the reasonableness of grounds for insecurity and the adequacy of any assurance offered are determined according to commercial standards.
Acceptance of any improper delivery or payment does not prejudice the aggrieved party's right to demand adequate assurance of future performance.

After receipt of a justified demand, failure to provide within a reasonable time not exceeding thirty days such assurance of due performance as is adequate under the circumstances of the particular case is a repudiation of the contract.
c: Commercial parties bargain for actual performance and a continuing sense of security that it will come, not just a promise plus a lawsuit. If a party's willingness or ability to perform declines materially, the other is threatened with losing much of its bargain: a seller should not have to manufacture or ship on credit to a shaky buyer, and a buyer relying on supplies cannot safely wait for the due date.

Three measures: (1) the aggrieved party may suspend its own performance and preparation, excused for necessary delay, until the situation clears; (2) it may require adequate assurance; (3) it may treat the contract as broken if the insecurity is not cleared up in a reasonable time - merging stoppage, credit-curtailment clauses, and anticipatory breach into one theory for all executory sales.

"Reasonable grounds" and "adequate assurance" are measured by commercial, not legal, standards, and good faith applies too. Grounds need not arise from the same contract: a buyer behind on its account under separate contracts, a seller making defective deliveries of precision parts to other buyers, or a manufacturer breaching a related exclusive-franchise agreement (Jay Dreher) can all give grounds. A report from an apparently trustworthy source that the seller shipped or plans to ship defective goods normally gives grounds - but a buyer who agreed to pay before inspection (C.I.F., cash against documents) cannot evade that risk by demanding assurance unless the report goes to a ground that would excuse payment.

Adequacy depends on the facts. A reputable seller's promise to fix a usable defect may be enough, while the same words from a known corner-cutter may need a guaranty or speedy replacement; where defects interfere with use, words alone are not enough without repair, replacement, allowance, or other cure. In the Corn Products example, false rumors plus the buyer's sudden failure to take its usual early-payment discount gave the seller grounds; but the seller's satisfaction must rest on reason, not be arbitrary or capricious, and a good banker's credit report would ordinarily be adequate assurance. Repeated delinquencies are cumulative, but repeated demands need increasingly obvious grounds.

Failure to give adequate assurance is a breach only "by repudiation," so it can be retracted under § 2-611 unless the aggrieved party has acted on it. The 30-day cap removes uncertainty about the reasonable time.

Clauses giving very broad powers to cancel or readjust on insecurity are limited by the nonwaivable good faith obligation. They can enlarge protection somewhat, fix the time to respond, or define adequate assurance in a commercially reasonable way, but clauses setting arbitrary standards are ineffective.
On records other than writings, see § 2-207, Comment 8.

statutes.t: Anticipatory Repudiation
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 6 - Breach, Repudiation and Excuse
x: When either party repudiates the contract with respect to a performance not yet due, the loss of which will substantially impair the value of the contract to the other, the aggrieved party may (a) for a commercially reasonable time await performance by the repudiating party; or (b) resort to any remedy for breach (§ 2-703 or § 2-711), even though it has notified the repudiating party that it would await performance and has urged retraction; and (c) in either case suspend its own performance or proceed under § 2-704 (seller's right to identify goods or salvage unfinished goods).
c: Repudiation centers on an overt communication of intention, or an action that makes performance impossible or shows a clear determination not to continue. When it substantially impairs the contract's value, the aggrieved party may sue at once or suspend and wait or negotiate - but if it waits beyond a commercially reasonable time, it cannot recover damages it should have avoided.

Performance need not be literally impossible: action that reasonably indicates rejection of the continuing obligation is enough, and failing to answer a justified § 2-609 demand within 30 days is a repudiation. Demanding more than the contract requires is not by itself a repudiation and does not cancel a plain expression of desire to perform; but a statement, fairly read, that a party will not perform except on conditions beyond the contract is a repudiation.

The test is substantial impairment of the value of the whole contract, as in § 2-612: whether material inconvenience or injustice will result if the aggrieved party must wait and receive an ultimate tender minus the repudiated part.

After repudiation, the aggrieved party may pick any remedy at once if it acts in good faith (§ 1-304). Silence or inaction leaves the matter open without misleading the repudiator, unless the aggrieved party took positive action that in good faith requires notice before it switches course.

statutes.t: Retraction of Anticipatory Repudiation
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 6 - Breach, Repudiation and Excuse
x: Until the repudiating party's next performance is due, it can retract its repudiation unless the aggrieved party has since the repudiation cancelled or materially changed its position or otherwise indicated that it considers the repudiation final.
Retraction may be by any method which clearly indicates to the aggrieved party that the repudiating party intends to perform, but must include any assurance justifiably demanded under § 2-609.
Retraction reinstates the repudiating party's rights under the contract, with due excuse and allowance to the aggrieved party for any delay caused by the repudiation.
c: The right to retract depends entirely on what the aggrieved party has done: once it has cancelled or materially changed position, retraction is impossible.

A repudiation is itself reasonable grounds for insecurity, so an effective retraction must include any assurance demanded. After a timely, unambiguous retraction, the aggrieved party should allow a reasonable time to work out assurance before cancelling.

statutes.t: "Installment Contract"; Breach
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 6 - Breach, Repudiation and Excuse
x: An "installment contract" is one which requires or authorizes the delivery of goods in separate lots to be separately accepted, even though the contract contains a clause "each delivery is a separate contract" or its equivalent.

The buyer may reject any installment which is nonconforming if the nonconformity substantially impairs the value of that installment and cannot be cured, or if the nonconformity is a defect in the required documents; but if the nonconformity does not fall within (3) and the seller gives adequate assurance of its cure, the buyer must accept that installment.

Whenever nonconformity or default with respect to one or more installments substantially impairs the value of the whole contract, there is a breach of the whole. But the aggrieved party reinstates the contract if it accepts a nonconforming installment without seasonably notifying of cancellation, or if it brings an action with respect only to past installments, or demands performance as to future installments.
c: The definition covers installment deliveries tacitly authorized by the circumstances or by either party's option.

Price apportionment uses the liberal test of what can be apportioned, including approximate apportionment subject to adjustment; a separate-payment clause is not essential, and the old "entire" vs. "divisible" contrast has no standing.
"Each delivery is a separate contract" clauses are not given their literal, legalistic effect; the single document and negotiation prevail.

Rejecting an installment requires substantial impairment of that installment, but the contract may require exact conformity if the need is made clear (expressly or by circumstances), with some basis in reason and without unfair surprise. Impairment may involve quality, time, quantity, assortment, and the like, judged by the contract's normal or known purposes. Document defects include a missing C.I.F. insurance document or a false bill of lading, though cure applies if proper documents are readily obtainable.

A curable installment must be accepted if the seller gives adequate assurance of cure (by price allowance, further delivery, or partial rejection). Good faith requires the buyer to make reasonable minor efforts, such as separating out an acceptable portion of an overshipment; materially burdensome cure falls on the seller.

Subsection (3) favors continuing the contract absent overt cancellation; suing only on past installments waives cancellation. Whether a defective installment justifies cancelling the future depends on whether it substantially impairs the value of the whole contract - not on whether it signals future defects. If only security about future installments is impaired, the remedy is a demand for adequate assurance, not cancellation. Defects in prior installments are cumulative, so accepting one does not wash out its defect.

A buyer may accept a seriously nonconforming installment and delay deciding whether to cancel while awaiting the seller's response, and a seller may withhold delivery pending payment for earlier ones; the reasonable time includes good faith negotiation, but the defaulting party may ask whether the contract is still in effect before performing further.
k: each delivery is a separate contract
substantially impairs the value of that installment
substantially impairs the value of the whole contract

statutes.t: Casualty to Identified Goods
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 6 - Breach, Repudiation and Excuse
x: Where the contract requires for its performance goods identified when the contract is made, and the goods suffer casualty without fault of either party before the risk of loss passes to the buyer, or in a proper case under a "no arrival, no sale" term (§ 2-324): (a) if the loss is total, the contract is avoided; and (b) if the loss is partial or the goods have so deteriorated as no longer to conform, the buyer may nevertheless demand inspection and at its option either treat the contract as avoided or accept the goods with due allowance from the contract price for the deterioration or the deficiency in quantity, but without further right against the seller.
c: When goods whose continued existence the agreement presupposes are destroyed without fault of either party, the buyer is released but may take what survives at a fair price adjustment. "Fault" includes negligence, not just willful wrong. The buyer may inspect to decide.

The section applies whether the goods were already destroyed at contracting (unknown to both) or destroyed later but before risk passed. It does not apply if risk had already passed to the buyer. The key question is whether the seller took responsibility for the goods' continued existence in proper condition through delivery.
Under a "no arrival, no sale" term, delay in arrival, like physical change, gives the buyer these options.
k: identified when the contract is made

statutes.t: Substituted Performance
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 6 - Breach, Repudiation and Excuse
x: Where without fault of either party the agreed berthing, loading, or unloading facilities fail, or an agreed type of carrier becomes unavailable, or the agreed manner of delivery otherwise becomes commercially impracticable, but a commercially reasonable substitute is available, the substitute performance must be tendered and accepted.

If the agreed means or manner of payment fails because of domestic or foreign governmental regulation, the seller may withhold or stop delivery unless the buyer provides a means or manner of payment which is commercially a substantial equivalent. If delivery has already been taken, payment by the means or in the manner provided by the regulation discharges the buyer's obligation unless the regulation is discriminatory, oppressive, or predatory.
c: Where agreed incidental facilities fail, a commercially reasonable substitute must be tendered and accepted. Unlike §§ 2-613 and 2-615 (which avoid the contract when a basic assumption fails), this section covers failures of incidental matters, not the heart of the deal. Compare a fire destroying the specific timber tract (excuse) with a canceled steamer sailing under an "f.o.b. Kosmos Steamer" term (substituted delivery at the dock). True commercial impracticability is required.
Substitution between buyer and seller does not change a bank's obligations under a letter of credit, which look only to the documents.

If payment fails due to regulation while the contract is executory on both sides, the seller may withdraw unless the buyer offers a commercial equivalent; once only the price debt remains, the buyer may pay as the regulation provides unless it is discriminatory, oppressive, or predatory.

statutes.t: Excuse by Failure of Presupposed Conditions
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 6 - Breach, Repudiation and Excuse
x: Preamble
Except so far as a seller may have assumed a greater obligation, and subject to § 2-614 (substituted performance):

Delay in delivery or non-delivery in whole or in part by a seller who complies with (b) and (c) is not a breach of its duty under a contract for sale if performance as agreed has been made impracticable by the occurrence of a contingency the non-occurrence of which was a basic assumption on which the contract was made, or by compliance in good faith with any applicable foreign or domestic governmental regulation or order, whether or not it later proves to be invalid.

Where the causes in (a) affect only a part of the seller's capacity to perform, it must allocate production and deliveries among its customers, but may at its option include regular customers not then under contract as well as its own requirements for further manufacture. It may allocate in any manner which is fair and reasonable.
The seller must notify the buyer seasonably that there will be delay or non-delivery and, when allocation is required under (b), of the estimated quota thus made available for the buyer.
c: The section excuses a seller whose performance has become commercially impracticable because of unforeseen supervening circumstances not within the parties' contemplation at contracting. Destruction of specific goods (§ 2-613) and substituted performance (§ 2-614) are separate.
The section does not try to list all contingencies; it is applied by its underlying reason and purpose.
The first test is the familiar "basic assumption." The added test of "commercial impracticability" (rather than impossibility or frustration) stresses the commercial character of the standard.

Increased cost alone does not excuse performance unless the rise is due to an unforeseen contingency that alters the essential nature of the performance. A rise or collapse in the market is not an excuse - that is exactly the business risk fixed-price contracts are meant to cover. But a severe shortage of raw materials or supplies from a contingency such as war, embargo, local crop failure, or unforeseen shutdown of major sources of supply, causing a marked increase in cost or preventing the seller from getting supplies, is within the section.

If an agreed exclusive source of supply fails through casualty, this section (not § 2-613) applies; the same is true for a source both parties contemplated. But there is no excuse unless the seller used all due measures to assure itself the source would not fail (Canadian Industrial Alcohol). An excused seller must turn over to the buyer its rights against the defaulting source, so it does not pocket an unearned windfall.
Where neither a flat "excuse" nor "no excuse" serves sense or justice, adjustment under good faith, insecurity and assurance, and equitable principles is called for.

Failure of conditions going to convenience or collateral values, rather than the practicability of the main performance, is not a complete excuse; good faith may justify delay for a good faith effort to readjust terms.

The exemption does not apply where the seller assumed a greater obligation, found in the express terms, the circumstances, or trade usage. A contingency sufficiently foreshadowed at contracting to be among the business risks fairly regarded as part of the dickered terms does not excuse. Express force majeure clauses are read with mercantile sense; this section sets a minimum standard beyond which agreement may not go.

A farmer selling crops from designated land may be excused on crop failure under § 2-613 or this section. A buyer's exemption in a requirements contract is governed by § 2-306. A manufacturer's contract to buy fuel or raw material is normally a general market deal not conditioned on its plant continuing, even if it says the supplies are for a particular contract; but where the buyer's contract is clearly tied to a specific venture (a war subcontract dependent on a terminable prime contract, a particular construction project), the buyer may be exempt.

Foreign and domestic regulations count equally, with no technical distinctions between law, regulation, and order; the seller's good faith belief in validity is the test. But governmental action excuses only if it truly supervenes beyond the seller's assumed risk, and a party that causes or colludes in the government action loses the excuse.

An excused seller must perform as far as the contingency permits and allocate fairly among customers, including regular spot customers and its own manufacturing needs. When prices have risen, good faith requires real care; in doubt, contract customers should be favored and supplies prorated evenly regardless of price.

statutes.t: Procedure on Notice Claiming Excuse
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 6 - Breach, Repudiation and Excuse
x: Where the buyer receives notification of a material or indefinite delay or an allocation justified under § 2-615, it may by written notification to the seller as to any delivery concerned (and, where the prospective deficiency substantially impairs the value of the whole contract under § 2-612, as to the whole): (a) terminate and thereby discharge any unexecuted portion of the contract; or (b) modify the contract by agreeing to take its available quota in substitution.
If after receiving such notification the buyer fails to modify the contract within a reasonable time not exceeding thirty days, the contract lapses with respect to any deliveries affected.
This section may not be negated by agreement except so far as the seller has assumed a greater obligation under § 2-615.
c: The section provides simple machinery for certainty about whether a supervening contingency excuses delay, discharges the contract, or leads to a waiver. The buyer may acquiesce, modifying the contract without consideration; otherwise it may terminate, and silence for up to 30 days operates as termination as to affected deliveries. An advance clause requiring the buyer to stand ready to take delivery whenever an excused seller can deliver is ineffective.
On records other than writings, see § 2-207, Comment 8.

statutes.t: Seller's Remedies on Discovery of Buyer's Insolvency
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 7 - Remedies
x: Where the seller discovers the buyer to be insolvent, it may refuse delivery except for cash, including payment for all goods previously delivered under the contract, and may stop delivery under § 2-705.

Where the seller discovers that the buyer has received goods on credit while insolvent, it may reclaim the goods upon demand made within ten days after the receipt; but if a misrepresentation of solvency was made to the particular seller in writing within three months before delivery, the ten-day limit does not apply. Otherwise the seller may not base a right to reclaim on the buyer's fraudulent or innocent misrepresentation of solvency or intent to pay.

The right to reclaim under (2) is subject to the rights of a buyer in ordinary course or other good faith purchaser under § 2-403. Successful reclamation excludes all other remedies with respect to the goods.
c: The seller may withhold or stop delivery except for cash on discovering insolvency, regardless of title, and stoppage extends to any bailee who has not yet attorned to the buyer.

Receiving goods on credit while insolvent is treated as a tacit misrepresentation of solvency, fraudulent as to that seller. Reclamation requires discovery and demand within ten days after receipt, unless there was a written misrepresentation of solvency addressed to that seller and dated within three months before delivery.
Because reclamation prefers the seller over other creditors, it bars the seller's other remedies as to those goods.
On records other than writings, see § 2-207, Comment 8.

statutes.t: Seller's Remedies in General
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 7 - Remedies
x: Where the buyer wrongfully rejects or revokes acceptance of goods, or fails to make a payment due on or before delivery, or repudiates with respect to a part or the whole, then with respect to any goods directly affected and, if the breach is of the whole contract (§ 2-612), also with respect to the whole undelivered balance, the aggrieved seller may: (a) withhold delivery of such goods; (b) stop delivery by any bailee (§ 2-705); (c) proceed under § 2-704 as to goods still unidentified to the contract; (d) resell and recover damages (§ 2-706); (e) recover damages for non-acceptance (§ 2-708) or in a proper case the price (§ 2-709); (f) cancel.
c: This is an index of the seller's remedies. Article 2 rejects any doctrine of election of remedies; the remedies are cumulative, and whether pursuing one bars another depends on the facts.
A breach may affect one lot or the whole contract; § 2-612 decides when the seller may act as to all the goods.
"Fails to make a payment due" includes a dishonored check, non-acceptance of a draft, and failure to furnish an agreed letter of credit.
Remedies are liberally administered, and rights are enforceable by action unless otherwise specified (§ 1-305).

statutes.t: Seller's Right to Identify Goods to the Contract Notwithstanding Breach or to Salvage Unfinished Goods
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 7 - Remedies
x: An aggrieved seller under § 2-703 may (a) identify to the contract conforming goods not already identified if, when it learned of the breach, they were in its possession or control; (b) treat as the subject of resale goods which have demonstrably been intended for the particular contract even though they are unfinished.

Where the goods are unfinished, an aggrieved seller may, in the exercise of reasonable commercial judgment for the purposes of avoiding loss and of effective realization, either complete the manufacture and wholly identify the goods to the contract, or cease manufacture and resell for scrap or salvage value, or proceed in any other reasonable manner.
c: The seller may identify conforming finished goods at the time of breach regardless of resalability, and use reasonable judgment about unfinished goods - making them available for resale (the primary remedy) or, where resale is impracticable, for an action for the price.

The seller may complete manufacture or procurement unless reasonable commercial judgment, based on the facts when it learns of the breach, makes clear completion will materially increase damages. The burden is on the buyer to show the seller's choice to complete was commercially unreasonable.

statutes.t: Seller's Stoppage of Delivery in Transit or Otherwise
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 7 - Remedies
x: The seller may stop delivery of goods in the possession of a carrier or other bailee when it discovers the buyer to be insolvent (§ 2-702), and may stop delivery of carload, truckload, planeload, or larger shipments when the buyer repudiates or fails to make a payment due before delivery, or if for any other reason the seller has a right to withhold or reclaim the goods.

As against the buyer, the seller may stop delivery until (a) receipt of the goods by the buyer; (b) acknowledgment to the buyer by any bailee other than a carrier that it holds the goods for the buyer; (c) such acknowledgment by a carrier by reshipment or as a warehouse; or (d) negotiation to the buyer of any negotiable document of title covering the goods.

(a) To stop delivery, the seller must notify so as to enable the bailee by reasonable diligence to prevent delivery. (b) After notification, the bailee must hold and deliver the goods according to the seller's directions, but the seller is liable to the bailee for ensuing charges or damages. (c) If a negotiable document of title has been issued, the bailee need not obey a stop order until surrender of possession or control of the document. (d) A carrier that issued a non-negotiable bill of lading need not obey a stop order from anyone other than the consignor.
c: Stoppage applies to all bailees, and beyond insolvency, but only for large shipments (to limit the burden on carriers); a seller worried about credit can ship C.O.D. Stoppage for insecurity is a suspension; if assurance comes, the seller may not resell or divert. Improper stoppage can be a breach by the seller.
Receipt by a sub-purchaser to whom the seller shipped directly counts as receipt by the buyer. A carrier need not obey a stranger's stop order, but the seller's right against the buyer remains.
A diversion incident to the original transport, or exchange bills naming the buyer's agent, is not a "reshipment."
A bailee need obey a stop order only on surrender of any negotiable document.
The seller bears the carrier's charges and losses from obeying its orders.
After effective stoppage, the seller's rights are as if no delivery had been made.

statutes.t: Seller's Resale Including Contract for Resale
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 7 - Remedies
x: Under the conditions of § 2-703, the seller may resell the goods concerned or the undelivered balance. Where the resale is made in good faith and in a commercially reasonable manner, the seller may recover the difference between the resale price and the contract price, together with any incidental damages (§ 2-710), but less expenses saved in consequence of the buyer's breach.

Except as provided in (3) or unless otherwise agreed, resale may be at public or private sale, including by one or more contracts to sell or by identification to an existing contract of the seller. It may be as a unit or in parcels, at any time and place and on any terms, but every aspect of the sale - method, manner, time, place, and terms - must be commercially reasonable. The resale must be reasonably identified as referring to the broken contract, but the goods need not exist or have been identified before the breach.
Where the resale is at private sale, the seller must give the buyer reasonable notification of its intention to resell.

Where the resale is at public sale: (a) only identified goods can be sold, unless there is a recognized market for public sale of futures in goods of the kind; (b) it must be made at a usual place or market for public sale if one is reasonably available and, except for goods that are perishable or threaten to decline in value speedily, the seller must give the buyer reasonable notice of the time and place; (c) if the goods are not within view of those attending, the notice must state where they are and provide for reasonable inspection by prospective bidders; and (d) the seller may buy.
A purchaser who buys in good faith at a resale takes the goods free of any rights of the original buyer even though the seller fails to comply with one or more requirements of this section.

The seller is not accountable to the buyer for any profit made on resale. A person in the position of a seller (§ 2-707), or a buyer who has rightfully rejected or justifiably revoked acceptance, must account for any excess over its security interest (§ 2-711(3)).
c: The only condition to resale is the buyer's breach (including anticipatory repudiation) under § 2-703 or insolvency; old technical conditions are replaced by commercial reasonableness. Goods not yet existing or identified at breach may be resold.

The seller must act in good faith and in a commercially reasonable manner; failing that, it loses this measure and is relegated to § 2-708. The seller resells for its own benefit to fix damages, not as the buyer's agent.
If the standard is met, resale price controls; market price evidence is relevant only to whether the resale was commercially reasonable. Whether title had passed does not matter.

Resale should realize as high a price as possible. "Public" sale means auction; "private" sale means solicitation and negotiation, directly or through a broker. Choose according to the goods and trade practice.
The time for resale is a commercially reasonable time after breach, depending on the goods and the market; the place is wherever is commercially reasonable, not necessarily the agreed delivery place.
The seller may depart from the original contract terms to the extent commercially reasonable.
Future goods repudiated before they exist can be "resold" by contracts to sell; goods identified after breach can be resold if they conform.

Private sale requires reasonable notice of intent to resell (not time and place). Public sale requires reasonable notice of time and place so the buyer can bid or bring bidders, except for perishables.

A public sale must be at a usual market if reasonably available (transport costs are incidental damages); otherwise at an advertised place bidders may reasonably attend. Unidentified goods can be sold at public sale only as futures in a recognized futures market. The seller may bid, which helps the buyer by raising the price.
A good faith purchaser at resale takes good title even if the seller did not follow this section.
The seller keeps any resale profit; a person in the position of a seller or a rejecting buyer resells only to realize its security interest and must account for any excess.

statutes.t: Seller's Damages for Non-acceptance or Repudiation
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 7 - Remedies
x: Subject to (2) and to § 2-723 (proof of market price), the measure of damages for non-acceptance or repudiation by the buyer is the difference between the market price at the time and place for tender and the unpaid contract price, together with any incidental damages (§ 2-710), but less expenses saved in consequence of the buyer's breach.

If the measure in (1) is inadequate to put the seller in as good a position as performance would have done, the measure of damages is the profit (including reasonable overhead) which the seller would have made from full performance by the buyer, together with any incidental damages (§ 2-710), due allowance for costs reasonably incurred, and due credit for payments or proceeds of resale.
c: Damages are measured by the current market price at the time and place for tender, determined by the tender rules and shipping terms (F.O.B., C.I.F., and so on). If there is no market price there, a substitute market may be shown under § 2-723, and § 2-724 eases proof of market quotations.

Lost profit (including reasonable overhead), together with limiting price actions to cases where resale is impracticable, eliminates unfair and wasteful results for fixed-price goods. It applies in all appropriate cases, including all standard-priced goods (the "lost volume" seller): normally list price less the dealer's cost, or list price less the manufacturer's cost. A history of earnings is not required, especially for a new venture.
The seller may always recover incidental damages.

statutes.t: Action for the Price
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 7 - Remedies
x: When the buyer fails to pay the price as it becomes due, the seller may recover, together with incidental damages under § 2-710, the price (a) of goods accepted or of conforming goods lost or damaged within a commercially reasonable time after risk of their loss has passed to the buyer; and (b) of goods identified to the contract if the seller is unable after reasonable effort to resell them at a reasonable price or the circumstances reasonably indicate that such effort will be unavailing.

A seller suing for the price must hold for the buyer any goods identified to the contract and still in its control, except that if resale becomes possible it may resell them at any time before collecting the judgment. Net resale proceeds must be credited to the buyer, and payment of the judgment entitles the buyer to any goods not resold.

After the buyer has wrongfully rejected or revoked acceptance, failed to make a payment due, or repudiated (§ 2-610), a seller held not entitled to the price shall nevertheless be awarded damages for non-acceptance under § 2-708.
c: Neither passing of title nor a fixed payment date matters to a price action now.
The price action is generally limited to cases where resale is impracticable, except where the buyer accepted the goods or they were destroyed after risk passed to the buyer.

An objective test replaces "not readily resalable": a reasonable effort to resell at a reasonable price must actually be made, or the circumstances must reasonably indicate it would fail (for example, specially made goods).
A buyer's default on an agreed advance is a breach of a collateral financing obligation, not a price claim.
"Goods accepted" excludes goods whose acceptance was justifiably revoked.
The list of cases where a price action lies is exhaustive.
If the price claim fails, the seller may recover § 2-708 damages in the same action.

statutes.t: Seller's Incidental Damages
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 7 - Remedies
x: Incidental damages to an aggrieved seller include any commercially reasonable charges, expenses, or commissions incurred in stopping delivery, in the transportation, care, and custody of goods after the buyer's breach, in connection with return or resale of the goods, or otherwise resulting from the breach.
c: The seller is reimbursed for expenses reasonably incurred because of the buyer's breach. The list states the normal additional items but is meant to allow all commercially reasonable expenditures. (Article 2 gives the seller no express right to consequential damages.)

statutes.t: Buyer's Remedies in General; Buyer's Security Interest in Rejected Goods
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 7 - Remedies
x: Where the seller fails to make delivery or repudiates, or the buyer rightfully rejects or justifiably revokes acceptance, then as to any goods involved, and as to the whole if the breach goes to the whole contract (§ 2-612), the buyer may cancel and, whether or not it has done so, may in addition to recovering so much of the price as has been paid (a) "cover" and have damages under § 2-712 as to all the goods affected, whether or not identified; or (b) recover damages for non-delivery under § 2-713.

Where the seller fails to deliver or repudiates, the buyer may also (a) if the goods have been identified, recover them under § 2-502; or (b) in a proper case obtain specific performance or replevy the goods under § 2-716.

On rightful rejection or justifiable revocation of acceptance, a buyer has a security interest in goods in its possession or control for any payments made on their price and any expenses reasonably incurred in their inspection, receipt, transportation, care, and custody, and may hold and resell them in like manner as an aggrieved seller (§ 2-706).
c: This indexes the remedies of a buyer who has not accepted or who has justifiably revoked: (1) money remedies, (2) remedies reaching the goods. Remedies for accepted goods are in § 2-714. A proper cure under § 2-508 can preclude these remedies, except for delay.

A buyer who paid part of the price (including by draft or note) or incurred listed expenses may hold and resell rejected goods like a seller, but may keep only the price paid and handling costs - no profit, and not an amount it thinks adequate for damages. Reselling does not impair the right to cover or non-delivery damages.
Remedies are liberally administered (§ 1-305).

statutes.t: "Cover"; Buyer's Procurement of Substitute Goods
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 7 - Remedies
x: After a breach within § 2-711, the buyer may "cover" by making in good faith and without unreasonable delay any reasonable purchase of, or contract to purchase, goods in substitution for those due from the seller.

The buyer may recover from the seller as damages the difference between the cost of cover and the contract price, together with any incidental or consequential damages (§ 2-715), but less expenses saved in consequence of the seller's breach.
Failure of the buyer to effect cover within this section does not bar it from any other remedy.
c: Cover lets the buyer get the goods it needs; it is the buyer's counterpart to the seller's resale.

Cover may be a series of contracts; substitute goods need not be identical, only commercially usable as reasonable substitutes; credit or delivery terms may differ if reasonable. The test is whether the buyer acted in good faith and reasonably at the time and place; it does not matter that hindsight shows a cheaper or better way. "Without unreasonable delay" still allows time to look around and decide how best to cover.

Cover is not mandatory; the buyer may choose § 2-713 market damages instead. But consequential damages are limited to those that could not reasonably have been prevented by cover (§ 2-715(2)(a)), and inability to cover is a condition to replevin (§ 2-716(3)).
Cover is available to consumers as well as merchants.

statutes.t: Buyer's Damages for Non-delivery or Repudiation
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 7 - Remedies
x: Subject to § 2-723 (proof of market price), the measure of damages for non-delivery or repudiation by the seller is the difference between the market price at the time when the buyer learned of the breach and the contract price, together with any incidental and consequential damages (§ 2-715), but less expenses saved in consequence of the seller's breach.
Market price is determined as of the place for tender or, in cases of rejection after arrival or revocation of acceptance, as of the place of arrival.
c: The yardstick is the market where the buyer would have covered: the place of tender (or place of arrival for rejection or revocation after arrival), at the time the buyer learned of the breach.
The market price is for goods of the same kind in the same branch of trade.

If the market price is hard to prove, § 2-723 allows a comparable market or spot-sale evidence. If no market price exists because of scarcity, that usually makes a good case for specific performance; opinion evidence on value may be admitted and consequential damages construed liberally.
Expenses saved by the breach are deducted.
This remedy is completely alternative to cover and applies only when and to the extent the buyer has not covered.

statutes.t: Buyer's Damages for Breach in Regard to Accepted Goods
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 7 - Remedies
x: Where the buyer has accepted goods and given notification (§ 2-607(3)), it may recover as damages for any nonconformity of tender the loss resulting in the ordinary course of events from the seller's breach, as determined in any manner which is reasonable.

The measure of damages for breach of warranty is the difference at the time and place of acceptance between the value of the goods accepted and the value they would have had if they had been as warranted, unless special circumstances show proximate damages of a different amount.
In a proper case any incidental and consequential damages under § 2-715 may also be recovered.
c: This covers a buyer who accepted and can no longer revoke. A buyer still owing part of the price may also deduct damages under § 2-717. Failing to give notice under § 2-607(3) bars both remedies.
"Nonconformity" includes breach of warranty and any other failure to perform contract obligations; loss is recovered "in any manner which is reasonable."

The value-difference measure in (2) is standard but not exclusive (cost of repair is a common proxy). It uses the place of acceptance rather than the place of tender. If the defect would have justified revocation, the time and place of acceptance is when the buyer decided not to revoke.
Incidental and consequential damages usually accompany this claim; see § 2-715.

statutes.t: Buyer's Incidental and Consequential Damages
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 7 - Remedies
x: Incidental damages resulting from the seller's breach include expenses reasonably incurred in inspection, receipt, transportation, and care and custody of goods rightfully rejected, any commercially reasonable charges, expenses, or commissions in connection with effecting cover, and any other reasonable expense incident to the delay or other breach.

Consequential damages resulting from the seller's breach include (a) any loss resulting from general or particular requirements and needs of which the seller at the time of contracting had reason to know and which could not reasonably be prevented by cover or otherwise; and (b) injury to person or property proximately resulting from any breach of warranty.
c: Incidental damages reimburse reasonable expenses of handling rightfully rejected (or revocable) goods and of effecting cover. The list is illustrative, not exhaustive.

The "tacit agreement" test for consequential damages is rejected. The common law "reason to know" (Hadley v. Baxendale) rule is followed, but recovery is barred unless the buyer could not reasonably have prevented the loss by cover or otherwise - the buyer must first try in good faith to minimize damages.

Absent excuse under § 2-615, the seller is liable for consequential damages whenever it had reason to know the buyer's general or particular requirements at contracting; no conscious acceptance of an insurer's liability is required. Particular needs generally must be made known; general needs rarely need to be. A seller that does not want this risk can limit remedies under § 2-719.
The buyer bears the burden of proving the extent of consequential loss, but mathematical precision is not required; loss may be determined in any reasonable manner.

Injury "proximately" resulting from breach of warranty: if the buyer used the goods without an inspection that it would have been reasonable to make, or used them after discovering the defect, the injury does not proximately result from the breach.
When goods are sold to a reseller, resale is a requirement the seller has reason to know of, so lost resale profits may be consequential damages.
k: could not reasonably be prevented by cover

statutes.t: Buyer's Right to Specific Performance or Replevin
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 7 - Remedies
x: Specific performance may be decreed where the goods are unique or in other proper circumstances.
The decree may include terms and conditions as to payment of the price, damages, or other relief as the court may deem just.

The buyer has a right of replevin for goods identified to the contract if after reasonable effort it is unable to effect cover or the circumstances reasonably indicate that such effort will be unavailing, or if the goods have been shipped under reservation and satisfaction of the security interest in them has been made or tendered. For goods bought for personal, family, or household purposes, the buyer's right of replevin vests upon acquisition of a special property, even if the seller had not then repudiated or failed to deliver.
c: Prior policy continues, but Article 2 encourages a more liberal attitude toward specific performance of sales contracts, within the court's discretion.

Uniqueness is judged by the total situation, not just whether goods were specific at contracting. Output and requirements contracts with a particular or peculiarly available source or market are today's typical case (rather than heirlooms and art). Relief may also be granted "in other proper circumstances," and inability to cover is strong evidence of them.

Replevin is available for identified goods when cover is reasonably unavailable, in addition to § 2-502. For consumer goods, the right vests on identification, so the buyer takes free of a later-attaching security interest created by the seller.
The buyer's rights to the goods parallel the seller's right to the price.
If a negotiable document of title is outstanding, replevin runs against the document.

statutes.t: Liquidation or Limitation of Damages; Deposits
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 7 - Remedies
x: Damages for breach by either party may be liquidated in the agreement, but only at an amount which is reasonable in light of the anticipated or actual harm caused by the breach, the difficulties of proof of loss, and the inconvenience or nonfeasibility of otherwise obtaining an adequate remedy. A term fixing unreasonably large liquidated damages is void as a penalty.

Where the seller justifiably withholds delivery because of the buyer's breach, the buyer is entitled to restitution of any amount by which its payments exceed (a) the amount the seller is entitled to under a valid liquidated damages term under (1), or (b) absent such a term, twenty percent of the value of the total performance for which the buyer is obligated, or $500, whichever is smaller.

The buyer's right to restitution under (2) is subject to offset to the extent the seller establishes (a) a right to recover damages under Article 2 provisions other than (1), and (b) the amount or value of any benefits received by the buyer directly or indirectly by reason of the contract.

Where a seller has received payment in goods, their reasonable value or the proceeds of their resale count as payments under (2); but if the seller has notice of the buyer's breach before reselling goods received in part performance, its resale is subject to § 2-706.
c: Liquidated damages clauses are allowed when reasonable in the circumstances, judged by the listed factors. An unreasonably large amount is void as a penalty; an unreasonably small amount may be struck as unconscionable under § 2-302.

Subsection (2) rejects forfeiture of a buyer's payments unless the amount kept is a reasonable liquidation of damages, except for small deposits (20% of the price or $500, whichever is smaller). It applies to any deposit, down payment, or part payment. For trade-ins resold before the breach, the amount actually received counts as the deposit; if the seller knows of the breach before reselling a trade-in, it must follow § 2-706.

statutes.t: Contractual Modification or Limitation of Remedy
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 7 - Remedies
x: Subject to (2) and (3) and to § 2-718: (a) the agreement may provide for remedies in addition to or in substitution for those in Article 2 and may limit or alter the measure of damages recoverable, as by limiting the buyer's remedies to return of the goods and repayment of the price or to repair and replacement of nonconforming goods or parts; and (b) resort to a remedy as provided is optional unless the remedy is expressly agreed to be exclusive, in which case it is the sole remedy.
Where circumstances cause an exclusive or limited remedy to fail of its essential purpose, remedy may be had as provided in the UCC.

Consequential damages may be limited or excluded unless the limitation or exclusion is unconscionable. Limitation of consequential damages for injury to the person in the case of consumer goods is prima facie unconscionable, but limitation of damages where the loss is commercial is not.
c: Parties may shape their remedies, and reasonable limits are enforced. But it is of the very essence of a sales contract that at least minimum adequate remedies be available - a fair quantum of remedy for breach. An unconscionable limitation is struck and the Code remedies apply as if it never existed. Under (2), an apparently fair clause that, because of circumstances, fails in its purpose or deprives a party of the substantial value of the bargain (for example, a repair-or-replace remedy when the seller cannot or will not repair) must give way to the general remedies.
Remedy clauses are presumed cumulative, not exclusive; an exclusive (sole) remedy must be clearly expressed.

Clauses limiting or excluding consequential damages are valid unless they operate unconscionably; they are an allocation of unknown or undeterminable risks. The seller may also disclaim warranties under § 2-316.

statutes.t: Who Can Sue Third Parties for Injury to Goods
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 7 - Remedies
x: Where a third party so deals with goods identified to a contract for sale as to cause actionable injury to a party to that contract: (a) a right of action against the third party is in either party who has title to, or a security interest, special property, or insurable interest in, the goods; and if the goods have been destroyed or converted, a right of action is also in the party who bore the risk of loss under the contract or has since assumed that risk; (b) if at the time of injury the plaintiff did not bear the risk of loss as against the other party and they have no arrangement for disposing of the recovery, its suit or settlement is, subject to its own interest, as a fiduciary for the other party; (c) either party may with the other's consent sue for the benefit of whom it may concern.
c: The section extends the real-party-in-interest principle. It applies only after identification; before that, only the seller can sue. Between identification and final acceptance (or after revocation) both parties may be able to sue, and even after acceptance both may if the seller kept possession or another interest.

statutes.t: Statute of Limitations in Contracts for Sale
statutes.part: Article 2, Part 7 - Remedies
x: An action for breach of any contract for sale must be commenced within four years after the cause of action has accrued. By the original agreement the parties may reduce the period of limitation to not less than one year but may not extend it.

A cause of action accrues when the breach occurs, regardless of the aggrieved party's lack of knowledge of the breach. A breach of warranty occurs when tender of delivery is made, except that where a warranty explicitly extends to future performance of the goods and discovery of the breach must await the time of such performance, the cause of action accrues when the breach is or should have been discovered.

Where an action commenced within the time limited by (1) is terminated so as to leave available a remedy by another action for the same breach, the other action may be commenced after the limitation period expires and within six months after the first action ends, unless the termination resulted from voluntary discontinuance or dismissal for failure or neglect to prosecute.
This section does not alter the law on tolling and does not apply to causes of action that accrued before it took effect.
c: A uniform four-year period replaces varying state limitation periods, helping businesses operating nationwide; four years fits normal commercial record-keeping. The parties may shorten the period to no less than one year in the original agreement but may not lengthen it. Accrual is at breach - for warranties, at tender of delivery - except for a warranty that explicitly extends to future performance. Subsection (3) is a savings clause for refiling, and (4) leaves state tolling law intact.

statutes.t: Scope (excerpt)
statutes.part: Article 9 - Secured Transactions (excerpts)
x: Except as provided in (c) and (d), Article 9 applies to a transaction, regardless of its form, that creates a security interest in personal property or fixtures by contract.
It also applies to a sale of accounts, chattel paper, payment intangibles, or promissory notes; to a consignment; and to security interests arising under §§ 2-401, 2-505, 2-711(3), or 2A-508(5).

Article 9 does not apply to, among other things: (4) a sale of accounts or similar rights as part of a sale of the business out of which they arose; (5) an assignment for collection only; (6) an assignment of a right to payment under a contract to an assignee that is also obligated to perform under the contract; (7) an assignment of a single account or similar right in full or partial satisfaction of a preexisting debt.
statutes.note: Only the subsections cited in the outline are summarized. In this course: a sale that is really a secured loan is governed by Article 9, not Article 2 (§ 2-102(3)), and Article 9's anti-assignment override does not reach an assignment of a right to payment to an assignee that must also perform the contract (§ 9-109(d)(6)), so ordinary assignment law and § 2-210 govern there.

statutes.t: Discharge of Account Debtor; Terms Restricting Assignment (excerpt)
statutes.part: Article 9 - Secured Transactions (excerpts)
x: Subject to (b)-(i), an account debtor (for example, a buyer that owes for goods) may discharge its obligation by paying the assignor until, but not after, it receives a notification, authenticated by the assignor or the assignee, that the amount due has been assigned and that payment is to be made to the assignee. After receiving the notification, the account debtor may discharge its obligation only by paying the assignee; paying the assignor no longer discharges it.

Except as provided in (e) and (k) and §§ 2A-303 and 9-407, and subject to (h), a term in an agreement between an account debtor and an assignor is ineffective to the extent that it (1) prohibits, restricts, or requires the account debtor's consent to the assignment or transfer of, or the creation, attachment, perfection, or enforcement of a security interest in, the account; or (2) provides that such an assignment or security interest may give rise to a default, breach, right of recoupment, claim, defense, termination, or remedy.
statutes.note: Cited with § 2-210(2): a seller's right to be paid for goods (an "account") stays assignable even if the sales contract forbids assignment.

statutes.t: Disposition of Collateral After Default (excerpt)
statutes.part: Article 9 - Secured Transactions (excerpts)
x: A contract for sale, lease, license, or other disposition of collateral includes the warranties relating to title, possession, quiet enjoyment, and the like which by operation of law accompany a voluntary disposition of property of that kind.

A secured party may disclaim or modify those warranties (1) in a manner that would be effective in a voluntary disposition of that kind of property; or (2) by communicating to the purchaser a record evidencing the contract for disposition and including an express disclaimer or modification.

A record is sufficient to disclaim warranties under (e) if it says "There is no warranty relating to title, possession, quiet enjoyment, or the like in this disposition" or uses words of similar import.
statutes.note: Cited with § 2-312, Comment 5: unlike a sheriff's sale, a secured party's foreclosure sale of goods carries title warranties unless properly disclaimed.

sections.title: I. The UCC & Which Law Governs
The UCC and the common law
sections.html:
• What it is: a model code (Uniform Law Commission (ULC) + American Law Institute (ALI)) adopted by the states to standardize commerce and protect those in business transactions. Not law until enacted; check each state's version. Louisiana never enacted Art. 2/2A.
  • § 1-103(a) purposes (construe liberally to promote): (1) simplify, clarify, modernize commercial law; (2) permit continued expansion of commercial practices through custom, usage, and agreement; (3) make the law uniform among jurisdictions.
  • § 1-103(b): unless displaced by a particular UCC provision, common law and equity (capacity, agency, estoppel, fraud, misrepresentation, duress, coercion, mistake, bankruptcy, other validating/invalidating causes) supplement the Code.
  • Sales law is broader than commercial law — buying and selling goods by individuals, businesses, and others; a cumulative subject, not one law.
  • Role of sales systems: bring buyers and sellers together; supply standard terms; supply mechanisms for performing; supply mechanisms for resolving disputes.
  • Recurring themes: certainty · responsiveness · laissez-faire · simplicity · efficiency · international.

sections.title: Statutory interpretation (slides + text)
sections.html:
• Three rules: (1) read it all, then read it again — parse grammar, find the pauses, test hypotheticals; (2) find the definitions (§ 1-201 for all Articles; §§ 2-103 to 2-106; "purchase" includes a gift; "goods" includes unborn animals); (3) read in context of the provision's and the Code's purposes.
  • Then consult: Official Comments (most important aid, but not law — the text controls if they conflict), case law (other states are persuasive), treatises, state legislative history, earlier drafts; last resort, a tie-breaker policy.
  • Keep the client's goals in view. Good drafting: understand the deal; know the rules and risk-allocation options; attention to detail; concise, clear, simple language — goal: an enforceable agreement that clearly reflects the deal.

sections.title: Is it a "good"? — § 2-105(1), § 2-107

Also includes unborn young of animals, growing crops, and things attached to realty under § 2-107.

sections.title: Hybrid transactions (goods + services/other property)
sections.html:
Test

Question

Notes

Predominant purpose (majority, pre-2022)

Is the predominant purpose goods or services? All-or-nothing.

Factors: contract language · nature of supplier's business · relative value of goods vs. services · whether applying Art. 2 makes sense. Hard to apply; why should services insulate goods from warranties?

Gravamen of the claim (Anthony Pools, Md.)

Does the claim relate to the goods or the services?

Anthony Pools (note case, casebook p. 24): an unmerchantable diving board, supplied under a pool-construction contract in which services predominated, caused personal injuries → Art. 2 applied to impose the merchantability warranty and to test the disclaimer. Outside class materials: the homeowner slipped off the board. Hard to apply (contact lenses — bad lens or bad exam?); multiple statutes of limitations may apply to one deal. Little traction.

2022 Amendments — § 2-102(2)

Two tiers

Goods predominate → Art. 2 applies. Goods don't predominate → only provisions relating primarily to the goods apply.

  • § 2-106(5) "hybrid transaction": a sale of goods plus services, a lease of other goods, or a sale/lease/license of non-goods property (provided by the seller).
  • Still apply when goods don't predominate (cmt. 5): warranties (§§ 2-312–2-318), tender & risk of loss, acceptance/rejection/cure, buyer's remedies for nondelivery/nonconforming goods. Don't apply: § 2-201, §§ 2-204–2-207, § 2-209.
  • Predominance factors (cmt. 3): agreement's language; share of price for the goods (an agreed allocation usually binds); parties' purposes; nature of businesses. Manufacturing services count toward goods; design services don't.
  • Problem 1-2 (Speedy Offset prints & binds 500 art books): printing/binding = services in manufacturing goods → goods predominate → Art. 2 applies; claims concern conformity of the books, so warranty rules apply either way.
  • Problem 1-4: Art. 2 governs merchant→merchant, merchant→consumer, consumer→merchant, and consumer→consumer (garage sale) — scope never depends on merchant status.
  • Disguised security interest: a "sale" with a mandatory repurchase at a higher price is really a secured loan → Art. 9, not Art. 2 (§ 2-102(3)(a)).

sections.title: Common law vs. UCC; agreement vs. contract
sections.html:
Common law

UCC Article 2

Mutual assent; based on promise

Based on bargain, as to goods

Mirror-image rule — acceptance must match the offer

Contract formed "in any manner sufficient to show agreement"; acceptance need not mirror

All material terms needed

Open terms OK; fewer formalities; many ways to form

  • "Agreement" (§ 1-201(b)(3)) = the parties' bargain in fact, from language and course of performance (CoP) / course of dealing (CoD) / usage of trade (UoT). "Contract" (§ 1-201(b)(12)) = the total legal obligation that results, as determined by the UCC and other law. The contract can be more (gap fillers, implied warranties) or less (statute of frauds (SOF), unconscionable term) than the agreement.
  • Questions to ask: (1) Offer? (common law — Restatement § 24: manifestation of willingness to bargain that justifies another in understanding assent is invited and will conclude it) (2) Firm offer by a merchant (§ 2-205)? (3) Properly accepted (§ 2-206)? (4) Do the terms conflict (§ 2-207)?

sections.title: § 2-204 — formation in general
sections.html:
rule

(1) Contract may be made in any manner sufficient to show agreement, including conduct by both parties. (2) OK even if the moment of making is undetermined. (3) Open terms don't defeat a contract if the parties intended to contract AND there is a reasonably certain basis for giving an appropriate remedy.

sections.title: § 2-206 — offer & acceptance
sections.html:
• (1)(a) Unless unambiguously indicated otherwise, acceptance in any reasonable manner and medium. (Offeror can still be "master of the offer.")
  • (1)(b) An order for prompt or current shipment may be accepted by a prompt promise to ship or by prompt shipment of conforming OR nonconforming goods — but shipping nonconforming goods is not an acceptance if seller seasonably notifies it's an accommodation. (No notice → acceptance and breach.)
  • (2) Where beginning performance is a reasonable mode of acceptance, an offeror not notified within a reasonable time may treat the offer as lapsed.

sections.title: § 2-205 — firm offers
sections.html:
rule

An offer by a merchant in a signed record that by its terms assures it will be held open is irrevocable without consideration for the time stated (or a reasonable time) — never more than 3 months. If the assurance is on a form supplied by the offeree, the offeror must separately sign it.

  • Common law: irrevocable only with consideration (option contract). Only the offeror must be a merchant.

sections.title: § 2-207 — battle of the forms
sections.html:
• (1) A definite and seasonable expression of acceptance (or written confirmation) is an acceptance even with additional/different terms, unless expressly made conditional on assent to them. → Abolishes mirror image & "last shot."
  • (2) Additional terms = proposals. Between merchants they become part of the contract unless (a) the offer expressly limits acceptance to its terms, (b) they materially alter it, or (c) objection is given within a reasonable time.
  • (3) If the writings don't form a contract but conduct recognizes one → contract on the terms where the writings agree + UCC gap fillers.
  • Three questions: (1) Agreement despite deviation? (2) Which terms control? (3) If writings fail, does conduct create a contract?
main case

Daitom, Inc. v. Pennwalt Corp. (10th Cir. 1984) — § 2-207 battle of the forms

Source: principal case, casebook pp. 47–57. Not named on the slides; the topic is covered at W1-S44 to S47.

Facts: Seller Pennwalt sent a typed proposal (the offer) to sell buyer Daitom two rotary vacuum dryers; its attached printed terms limited warranties and required any suit within 1 year of delivery. Daitom answered with its own purchase order (PO) — boilerplate on the back reserved "all of its rights and remedies available at law" and said acceptance was "expressly limited to such terms." The dryers were delivered in May 1977 but sat in crates while Daitom's plant was built; when finally run in June 1978 they were seriously defective. Daitom sued in March 1980 — too late under the 1-year term, timely under the UCC's 4 years.

Held: (1) The PO was an acceptance, not a counteroffer: "expressly conditional" requires the offeree to clearly say it won't proceed unless its terms are accepted (Dorton) — form language like "expressly limited to such terms" isn't enough. (2) The 1-year term and Daitom's reservation of its legal remedies (which impliedly reserved the statutory period) were different (conflicting) terms → knock-out rule (cmt. 6): both drop out, and the gap filler — § 2-725's 4-year statute of limitations (SOL) — applies. Summary judgment for Pennwalt reversed. (Dissent: would affirm — Daitom accepted Pennwalt's offer.)

Why it matters: the textbook illustration that § 2-207 abolished the mirror-image and "last shot" rules — a nonconforming acceptance still forms a contract, and when the forms conflict neither side's boilerplate wins; the UCC default does. The court stressed the 1-year period would have run before the machines were even installed.

  • Material alterations (cmt. 4): warranty disclaimers, 90–100% delivery guarantees where trade allows leeway, power to cancel on any late invoice, unusually short complaint periods. Not material (cmt. 5): reasonable force-majeure terms, customary complaint periods, interest on overdue invoices, limits on rejection within trade tolerances.
  • How UCC changes offer/acceptance: any reasonable medium (2-206(1)(a)); accept by shipping (2-206(1)(b)); firm offers (2-205); no mirror image (2-207(1)); confirmation = acceptance (2-207(1)).

sections.title: § 2-201(1) — the rule
sections.html:
rule

A contract for the sale of goods for $500 or more is not enforceable by action or defense unless there is a record (1) sufficient to indicate a contract for sale was made, (2) signed by the party against whom enforcement is sought (or its agent/broker). A record isn't insufficient because it omits or misstates a term, but the contract isn't enforceable beyond the quantity shown.

  • Only quantity is essential; price/delivery can be missing or wrong. "Record" includes email (2022 amendments; the Uniform Electronic Transactions Act (UETA) elsewhere); a typed name is a signature. Several papers can be read together if connected (Casazza).
  • Satisfying the SOF only opens the courthouse door — plaintiff must still prove the contract.
  • Flowchart: SOF applies? No → possible contract. Yes → sufficient signed record? Yes → possible contract. No → exception? Yes → possible contract; No → no enforceable contract.
